Giovanni Barra

She Did Not Love in Jest

Mother Rosa Gattorno, Foundress of the Daughters of Saint Anne

Second edition revised by Franco Molinari

Piero Gribaudi Editore, Turin · © 1968 and 1981 · Imprimatur: Mgr Santo Quadri, Pinerolo, 5 September 1968

Note on the text. Translated from the Italian text. Square brackets mark reconstructed words, doubtful passages [?] and gaps in the source.

“Daughter of Saint Anne, take up your cross, bow your head and go to work... the earth is vast and the field immense... never turn back... look at what is still to be done and never at what has been done... It is an ugly thing to believe one has done something.”

(from a letter of Mother Rosa Gattorno)

Pope John XXIII did not agree with the prophets of doom, who in every century foresee the end of the world and hear nothing but the scratching of Satan beneath the news of the day, the hoofbeats of the horses of the Apocalypse and the coming of the Antichrist.

If the devils run loose on the roads of the atheist and stupid century, there are also the angels of God and, among them, the Daughters of Saint Anne, who at the death of the Foundress (1900) had already swarmed out into the world and reached three continents.

The prophecy of Pius IX had been fulfilled, who on 3 January 1866 had foretold to Rosa Gattorno: “This Institute will spread rapidly, like the flight of the dove, to all parts of the world.”

The nineteenth century had seen the headlong collapse of all the religious Orders. First the Napoleonic hurricane had scattered the Congregations throughout Europe. Then in Italy the so-called suppression laws of the Risorgimento (1866-67) had done the rest, pulverizing every nucleus of consecrated life and confiscating the Church’s property, which is the patrimony of the poor.

Psalm 2 warns us, however, that before the treacherous and colossal conspiracy of a not very holy alliance, God laughs.

He laughs because He is the stronger. He is the stronger because He loves. The Daughters of Saint Anne take their first steps in Piacenza at the very moment when the police agents are putting the seals on the doors to close the convents. They are born like the kindly hand of God, stretched out towards the sick, the orphan girls, the girls in moral danger, the least of every region. While the Italian State, partly from the real need to shore up a catastrophic budget and partly from an artificial resurgence of livid and virulent anticlericalism, lays its hands on the goods of the religious Orders, Mother Gattorno “confiscates” seventy little orphan girls, daughters of the cholera. In Piacenza in June 1867 the deadly scourge had broken out, causing a slaughter of innocents. In a few weeks the small city was overflowing with 1,320 corpses.

Against that background of death there stands out the primacy of Love, who is God and who takes the side of life.

The simple people and even the Ghibelline authorities look with sympathy and esteem on that small group of women, who practice affectionate care and the free nursing of the sick in their homes.

Soon afterwards Mother Rosa starts a work for deaf-mute girls, drawing on her experience as an earthly mother (her little daughter Carlotta was a deaf-mute). The “little mutes”, who practice perennial praise of God in continuous prayer, are the lungs of the new-born institution and ensure its prodigious expansion. On 6 May 1900 the Foundress goes down to the grave, but the organized branches of her volcanic love for the least have already reached South America and Africa.

The flower of a renewed spring

The teeming Congregation of the Daughters of Saint Anne is not a solitary swallow. It is the flower of a renewed spring. The proliferation of numerous institutes of women becomes so vast that a joke goes round: among the very few things the good God does not know, in spite of His omniscience, is... the number of women’s Congregations. This vitality, all the more singular because it follows the storms of the suppressions, and all the more extraordinary because it runs parallel to rationalist positivism, has no equal in earlier ages and would deserve a thorough monograph: the nineteenth century records, in Italy alone, the rise of 183 new Institutes, among them the Daughters of Saint Anne. The figure seems enormous when one thinks of the 8 foundations of the sixteenth century, the 15 of the seventeenth, the 20 of the eighteenth. It is a pity that most of them take root in the North of the Peninsula. Here too a “southern question” arises, which is however on its way to a solution, since in the nineteenth century the distances grow shorter: to the 104 foundations of northern Italy there correspond 43 in central Italy and 35 in southern Italy. The geography of religious vocations, too, would deserve a historian’s sounding. What are the causes of this exuberant flowering?

Giacomo Martina answers: “Certainly two determining factors were the strong personality of the foundresses and of their directors, and the structure and purpose of the Institute, better suited to the times” (Various Authors, Chiesa e religiosità in Italia dopo l’Unità, Relazioni I, Milan, Vita e Pensiero, 1973, p. 201).

If on the historical level the diagnosis of the learned Jesuit historian hits the mark perfectly, in the perspective of faith it lets us glimpse, as in a watermark, the providential finger of God.

History is not explained by history. This supernatural principle, easy for a believer, was also grasped by a lay historian such as Giorgio Falco, one of the most acute Italian medievalists of the school of Croce. Going beyond Croce’s atheistic immanentism, he stressed that some enigmas of the human journey cannot be solved on the level of pure historicism, without openings towards heaven.

The suffering of the innocent (and how much of it there is!), the good that sometimes is born of evil, the survival of Christianity in spite of two thousand years of harassing wars, the unfolding of events almost always different from human plans: these are some of the countless mysteries that the historian without faith cannot decipher. These and very many other episodes cannot be explained without an invisible Director.

One of these mysterious facts, in which the parallelogram of the forces in play appears out of proportion to the result, is the silent germination of the Daughters of Saint Anne and their fruitful spread across the continents, as is plain from Barra’s biography, which is now published with additions and corrections made necessary by the progress of historical studies.

Father Tornatore

But is it really necessary to publish and republish biographies of the saints and of the servants of God?

It has been said that the blood of the martyrs is infinitely more important than the ink of writers.

The statement is correct, in that it expresses the Gospel category of witness. But I would not cast indiscriminate discredit on the “hack writers”. It is necessary that people see the good works of the protagonists of Love, so that they may glorify the Father, from whom every perfect gift comes down. It is true that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of new Christians: in our case the martyr, that is, the witness of Christ, was Rosa Gattorno, who “did not love in jest”. Saint Catherine’s cry, “blood and fire”, sums up the two poles of a life made of hair-shirts and tenderness, of sacrifices and burning charity, of crosses driven into the flesh and of heroic forgiveness of enemies (see the painful and exceptionally edifying episode which Barra tells so well in ch. VIII under the title “Signing in blood”, and which speaks of calumnies, of contempt, of real Judases, against whom the servant of God reacts with the only revenge of Christ, namely mercy). This edition has been changed in some fifteen pages (precisely pp. 59, 62, 72, 83, 84, 91, 97, 109, 110, 113, 122, 193). These are not radical restorations of the author’s thought, but clarifications and additions that could not be avoided after the recent critical findings that matured from the work of the Special Chapter held by the Daughters of Saint Anne between 1969 and 1971, and recorded in the official review “Virga Jesse”, as well as in the acts of the same Chapter.

The most important clarification, from the historical point of view, concerns the Vincentian Father Giovanni Battista Tornatore (1820-1895), to whom historiography, on the basis of scientifically reliable documents, has consequently awarded the title of co-founder, together with Gattorno, of the Daughters of Saint Anne. A title that was certainly not merely honorary, and that cost him the trial by fire of calumnies and harsh persecutions, a “reward”, accepted in faith but searing, for the fidelity with which he interpreted the one charism for whose fulfilment Providence had mysteriously chosen two persons.

Their meeting took place under the sign of what learned professors call, with academic solemnity, “the heteronomy of ends” (simple people translate that difficult formula into the fine proverb: “Man proposes and God disposes”).

Rosa Gattorno of Genoa did not know, and would never have thought of finding on her path, Father Tornatore, who lived in Piacenza with the double halo of saint and scholar, and held the chair of Theology in the prestigious Collegio Alberoni, known throughout the theological world for the review “Divus Thomas”.

The high intellectual stature of the man of God can be measured precisely by a series of articles that appeared in that authoritative periodical on a key problem of the doctrine of Saint Thomas, namely the mode of knowledge. The most substantial monograph, of more than 500 pages, on the Unity and Trinity of God and the Creating Principle of things, was to be published in Rome in 1878 at the expense of Gattorno herself. To his fame as a theologian was joined the good fragrance of Christ, so much so that he was nicknamed the saint of the Alberoni. As severe with himself as he was affable with others, he lived what would be the program of Pope John XXIII: “For myself I shall have the severity of a judge, for my neighbor the gentleness of a mother, for God the heart of a child.”

To reap in joy...

Rosa Gattorno, returning from Rome to her Genoa, made a chance stop in Piacenza. Circumstances are the sacrament of God’s will. The stop in Piacenza, from the human point of view, could be called accidental, but in the divine perspective it was the launching pad of the religious foundation and the point of reference for the meeting between those who would become the mother and the father of the Congregation.

Their communion of ideals could not have been more perfect in establishing the spirituality of the Daughters of Saint Anne, sisters of the Immaculate, brides of Christ. This spiritual tension flowed into the Rules of 1869, drawn up by Tornatore in total fidelity to the charism of the Institute. Still today they represent, as the Special Chapter of 1969 declared, the code of life of the religious Family, whose spirituality, soul and purpose they reflect, even after the new guidelines of Vatican II. It was precisely here that the calvary of Tornatore began, though he did not lose his way in the sometimes terrible sequence of his Way of the Cross. The first sorrowful station was the rejection of the Rules in Rome on scruples of form. The last searing wound of the Via dolorosa was the prohibition laid on Tornatore to go to the Mother House in Piacenza and to hear the confessions of his daughters. Anyone else would have collapsed under the gusts of that hailstorm of unjust persecutions and merciless misunderstandings. But the Father, austere with himself and indulgent with others, was able to see in the crucifying trial the mark of the nails, that is, the presence of Christ. Thus it was that the undertaking was all the more blessed by God the more it had been the target of the bitterness of earthly opponents.

Against the painful measure, which cut the father off from his family, the Bishop of Piacenza, G. B. Scalabrini, rose up and testified in favor of the “most distinguished churchman, rich in deep learning and eminent virtues”. After his death his spiritual daughters, already painfully struck by his absence, made constant and devout pilgrimages of gratitude to the tomb of Father Tornatore at S. Lazzaro Alberoni, and they have now obtained that his mortal remains should rest in a small catacomb-style chapel in the Mother House, where they await the resurrection. His return is a due homage to the memory of the one who sowed in tears, leaving to others the consolation of reaping in joy.

The biographer

The writer Fr Giovanni Barra (1914-1975) went down to the grave only a few years ago, and already in the summer of 1981, at the Center of spirituality of Pineta di Sortenna, Cardinal Michele Pellegrino was hoping for the opening of his process of beatification, observing: “For me he is a saint and he also reached the heights of the mystical way.”

By dint of keeping company with the saints, the lively biographer, who has given us the gripping film of Mother Rosa’s adventure, fortunately let himself be infected by the virus of heroic virtue.

The reliable and rigorous judgment of the Cardinal, who is also a university professor of early Christian literature and the editor of scrupulous critical editions, brings into focus the deep secret and the charm of the present biography, which has the brisk pace and the visual force of a film: the story does not even lack a touch of the thriller, when an attempt is made to poison the Foundress, or when in Foligno in the spring of 1873 the violent hands of “nun-eaters” smear the door of the very poor house with petrol and set it on fire, leaving writings full of insults and threats.

But this is not the chief merit of the book, which has a further title of no small worth in its wealth of data, facts and sayings. History is made with documents. And this history, though it does not pose as a scholarly narrative and lacks an apparatus of sources, is not a historical novel. It is a careful reconstruction, which is in good standing with truthfulness and does not indulge in hagiographical legends.

The reality of the figures is already eloquent enough: there is no need for the pen to draw baroque flourishes. When the Servant of God dies in 1900, she has promoted 318 houses in Italy. In America, 43. In Africa, 7. In all 368 houses, in which there are about 4,000 Daughters of Saint Anne.

This rapid expansion of the Institute could give rise to a dry piece of business book-keeping, with debits and credits, were it not for the seasoned craft of Fr Barra, who knows how to enliven this ledger of grace with winning titles (“Heaven is other people”), with apt images (“An illustrated edition of the Gospel”), with bold paradoxes (“It is not the path that is impossible, it is the impossible that becomes the path”), with sharp theological clarifications (“Our hope is Someone”), with tasty quotations from modern authors (from Chesterton to Péguy, from Santucci to Alessandro Pronzato).

In this last respect it may be said that every book of Barra’s is a tempting vineyard of literary passages, a fresh anthology, in which the best fragments of the religious literature of the last century find a place. He was a most prolific writer because he was an assiduous, diligent and intelligent reader. Just as Fr Barra quotes the thoughts of others with the honesty of quotation marks, without fear of disappearing, so in our case he has the good sense to let the protagonist speak, withdrawing behind the scenes and giving ample room to her flashing writings [?].

Friendship, the testing ground of a man

And here we touch the heart of the matter. Vittorio Morero, in an excellent biographical essay entitled “Don Barra ha giocato con Dio” (ed. Esperienze, Fossano), relates that the young priest had set out to “make friends”, following the psychological guidelines of an American book then in fashion. It was well for him that in the notebook of his personal friendships and of his historical acquaintances there are men such as the obedient prophet Fr Mazzolari, Father Bevilacqua the parish-priest cardinal, and strong women such as Armida Barelli, the treasurer of the Catholic University, and Rosa Gattorno. Saint Augustine says that a person is not known except through friendship (homo nisi per amicitiam cognoscitur).

Fr Barra translated the expression into modern terms: one must get inside other people’s skin. The simple secret of his apostolate among the young, as of his sketching of spiritual portraits of notable figures, was his ability to tune in to others.

It might have seemed that his meeting with the Servant of God Gattorno would not be easy, given the distance of mentality as well as of time. And yet the encounter could not have been gentler. The identification between the biographer and his subject found many points of support.

First of all, the lever that has the power to lift the world: prayer.

Fr Barra, a pioneer of the worker-priests and a popularizer of the most advanced French pastoral thought of Godin, Michonneau, Ancel and others, had in his last years come to the method of the knees. He always pressed the key of witness: for his profiles he always chose “the witnesses” of the Christ who is alive today. He preached that the only credible apologetics is fraternal love. His final goal he had translated into a volley of slogans, which are like pins for the soul: we become what we pray; pray more in order to love better; true prayer is not made of words but of glances; when I am with God I am doing the greatest work, because to pray is to love.

Some fragments of a diary seem to show that the prolific and jovial writer touched the summit of mysticism. He had become, according to his program, the vertical that reaches heaven and the horizontal that embraces the brethren. This conquest of the highest peak of contemplation coincides with the last stretch of his earthly journey (1969-1975) and is almost contemporary with the writing of the present biography.

For her part, Gattorno asked of the Daughters of Saint Anne five and a half hours of prayer every day. Without this green space of contemplation, her institution would have been suffocated by a polluting activism devoid of love. With the young and with the sisters, with priests and with lay people, Fr Barra played the card of religious totality, not in the sense of a reduction to the clerical sphere, but in the direction of a life lived in the fullness of self-gift. Here is another line of harmony with her who used to write the truth with the blood of her own veins and never ceased to repeat to her Daughters that our head is a Crucified One: and therefore they could not exchange the crown of thorns for a basket of cyclamens. High goals, not half measures. A Gospel not watered down. A complete Christianity, not sweetened. There are points of penitential rigorism in Gattorno’s development that the squeamish modern person will define as relics of the Middle Ages and expressions of masochism. But if our Leader has the cross for a throne, what do His followers expect? Whoever does not want to suffer does not know how to love. Mother Rosa, whose body is tormented by hair-shirts and by crosses literally driven into her flesh, teaches her Sisters to blaze with charity. Because, comments Fr Barra, if you do not burn with love, there is someone dying of cold. Our Churches sin by too much prudence, by good manners, by excessive wisdom.

Father Lebret, the chief inspirer of the encyclical Populorum Progressio, holds that folly belongs to the theological order and is a close relative of faith, hope and charity. To the young people who wished to enlist in the service of the third world he used to put this strange question: “Are you mad? O God, we need madmen in the present time.”

And the world will surrender to God

Rosa committed follies. Her follies are modelled on the folly of the cross. As when, with her confessor’s permission, she bound to her breast a Crucifix seven centimeters high and kept it pressed there day and night, so that it sank into her flesh and, when under obedience she had to remove it, she tore away shreds of tissue as well. But a sad Saint is a sorry Saint.

In Rosa Gattorno, penances and joy increase in step. Whoever comes near her is amazed to see her always serene and smiling.

On this point too the biography of the Foundress is something of the author’s autobiography. Long before post-conciliar theology discovered the vein of hope, Fr Barra had developed this Christian theme. Besides, the almost childlike radiance of his broad face, so like Pope John’s, was the sacrament of Christian cheerfulness.

How alike are the champions of the good God, even in their unrepeatable originality.

Fr Barra not only posted clusters of letters every day “to friends”, to young people, to readers who wanted explanations. He added a ninth beatitude to the eight of the Gospel: the beatitude of communicating with one’s brothers and sisters by letter. Blessed are letters, which allow us to be present to one another in spite of obstacles, and which oblige us to create within ourselves what is best in order to communicate it.

In the last period of her earthly life the Foundress, bound to immobility by illness, guides the Institute by correspondence. If it were gathered together, her vast collection of letters would be the most faithful mirror of her high-voltage spirituality. She spends hours dozing. As soon as she opens her eyes she turns them to the Crucifix and then writes letters to the distant Superiors. The last letter in her own hand is dated 1 May 1900. After that she is obliged to dictate.

She dies on the morning of 6 May 1900.

Religious women of the stamp of Gattorno and of the Daughters of Saint Anne fit Fr Barra’s apologetic style with exemplary exactness. Mother Rosa fascinates him because she is a strong woman and pulverizes the myth of the weaker sex; her Sisters are an explosive heritage and are capable of setting the world on fire with Christ.

The Sisters, it has been written, are the only Gospel that many people of today read.

The atheist stumbles upon the Sister at his children’s nursery school. The unbeliever meets her, smiling and attentive, in the hospital. The woman who killed her child in a fit of rage is comforted by the Sister in the cell of the women’s prison. The pagan leper sees her bend lovingly over his sores. An old unbeliever used to say: “I will be converted when I bump into a Christian.”

How many atheists will find Love and surrender to God with their hands raised, stumbling upon Mother Rosa and the Daughters of Saint Anne, evoked by the author with narrative originality and with autobiographical involvement.

Franco Molinari, Professor of Modern History at the Catholic University of the Sacred Heart

She was no longer young. The Daughters of Saint Anne, whom she had founded long before, had swarmed out almost everywhere.

One day, with a Genoese priest, she was walking along Via S. Rocchino, where there was a house once lived in by the Gattorno family and later, for a while, by the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Rosa Gattorno stopped. She looked at that house for a long time. A wave of memories filled her heart, and she said to the priest: “How many dances I danced in this house...”

Rosa Gattorno’s childhood and youth, then, had not been all holy water, spiritual exercises and pious ejaculations.

On the contrary, there was something violent, harsh and revolutionary in her veins. Not for nothing was she the niece, on her mother’s side, of Federico Campanella, a barricade-building follower of Mazzini and a revolutionary who one ill-fated day was caught up in a conspiracy against the government and barely saved his life by a daring escape.

Federico was studying law in Genoa. There he met Giuseppe Mazzini and drank in his anticlerical and revolutionary ideas.

With the brothers Jacopo and Giovanni Ruffini he worked hard to spread “Young Italy” and secretly prepared an uprising that was to break out in Genoa in the first months of 1833. But the news that a revolt was being plotted reached the ears of the civil and military authorities. How, no one ever knew: an indiscreet leak or betrayal?

The military authorities, under General Castelborgo, were merciless. The soldiers Antonio Gavotti, Giuseppe Biglia and Francesco Miglio were executed in the square of Cava on the morning of 15 June. One of Federico’s closest friends, Jacopo Ruffini, took his own life in the prison of the tower of the Ducal Palace; other well-to-do citizens were arrested and imprisoned.

Federico managed to elude the police search and took refuge in the Gattorno house at S. Maria delle Vigne, where the love of his sister and brother-in-law saved him. He disguised himself as a sailor and blackened his hands and face with tar. At the harbor no one recognized him; they took him for an ordinary cabin boy. So he managed to board a ship setting sail for Marseilles.

Federico wandered through Europe for fifteen years. He returned to Italy in 1848. In 1849 he was with Garibaldi’s men and with Mazzini in Rome, where he fought in the April and June battles at Porta S. Pancrazio, Villa Spada, Villa Corsini and on the barricades.

Anticlerical and a Freemason, head of Italian Freemasonry, a bitter enemy of the Church, he died in Florence on 9 December 1884 without being reconciled with God.

Rosa Gattorno’s brother, too, would stand out for his bitter anticlericalism. Yet this never kept him from holding his sister in great esteem and veneration. He could not understand her supernatural spirit, but he admired her lofty natural virtues — so much so that in a squabble in the Chamber in 1907 the Hon. Santini taunted him with the words: “Steward of the nuns of Via Merulana”.

A heated and unseemly incident followed. “Yes,” he retorted, “I had a sister who was a nun, but even so I have kept my principles against clericalism and against Catholics intact. So I should not be blamed for having had a sister who was a nun — who was, moreover, a holy woman.”

When Uncle Federico was smearing his face with tar in the Gattorno house, Rosa was two years old.

She was born in Genoa on 14 October 1831, in the Dealbertis house that can still be seen in Piazza S. Bernardo, marked by its sober eighteenth-century style. She was baptized on the day of her birth and given three names: Rosa, Benedetta, Maria. There were three brothers, three sisters and a half-sister whom her mother had had by her first marriage.

An early education in the nineteenth-century style: the boys at public schools, the girls at home with carefully chosen tutors. Social ties with the high nobility of Genoa. A markedly religious atmosphere at home. Perhaps a religious education not personal, motivated and owned enough? One would think so, hearing the haughtiness of the son Federico, who many years later would declare openly in Parliament that he was “against Catholics”.

But it is hard to pass judgment. In religious experience one meets the most unforeseeable things. The mystery of human freedom.

We know little of the religious formation given by her mother and the catechists, but what we know is illuminating enough. Her mother, for all the work she had at home, never failed to recite the Office of the Blessed Virgin every day. Certain sights are stamped on the minds and hearts of children so deeply, so vitally, that they become strength: idea-forces and image-forces.1

When Rosa Gattorno later named her Daughters after the Mother of Our Lady, was it the love of Our Lady planted in her heart by her mother that was at work? We think so. An episode worth recalling belongs to her childhood years.

Mgr Giovanni Maria Mastai Ferretti, the future Pope Pius IX, had recently been made Bishop of Imola. One day he passed through Genoa and stayed with the Gattorno family. He saw little Rosa and said to her mother with prophetic insight: “Take care of this child, who will have to come to me more than once.”

Thirty years later Rosa Gattorno would indeed meet Pius IX in Rome, in an audience decisive for the founding of the Daughters of Saint Anne. So began a close working relationship between the holy Pontiff and the Servant of God for the good of the Church. First Communion and Confirmation at eleven. From the informative Processes some facts emerge that mark the religious and moral life of her early adolescence.

First of all, the constant harmony between truth and charity, between humanity and religion.

“She knew how to go without what was superfluous and other pleasant things in order to satisfy even her brothers’ innocent whims.”2

She had managed, that is, to avoid the great reef on which the religious experience of young people often founders: the split between piety and charity. Girls who are angels in church but devils at home; good in church and hard on their companions. Piety is genuine only if it flowers from charity.

“I do not like,” writes Bruce Marshall, “the rhyme between a pure life and a hard life.”

“She was especially thoughtful in forestalling, hiding or softening anything that might distress her mother, who was extremely sensitive by nature.”

Love is made of little things. Love makes little things great. To one who loves, nothing is small. A flower is sometimes worth more than a check. A flower is always a declaration of love; a check sometimes barely pays a debt.

A poor man, frozen stiff, begs for alms. The passer-by rummages in his pocket and looks in his wallet: he has nothing. He shakes his hand warmly, wraps him in a kindly look and smiles at him. “That too is charity,” the poor man replies.

To the poor Rosa gives her smile, her time and whatever money she has.

Some years earlier her father had bought a house at S. Luca d’Albaro big enough for the whole family, who went there in the summer months. The poor of Albaro soon came to know the generous heart of this fifteen-year-old and often knocked at her door.

Then she began gathering the peasants’ children around her, teaching them a little catechism, playing with them and taking an interest in their lives.

“Among the children she looked like a mother hen with a brood of chicks,” her contemporaries said.

The poor, children, the afflicted of every kind: her world.

The whole world of the Daughters of Saint Anne is already there in embryo.

The Gattornos used to end their holidays at S. Luca d’Albaro on All Souls’ Day.

The holidays, spent under the sign of charity, ended under the sign of charity.

On that day a great crowd of poor people gathered at the Gattorno house. “For the souls in Purgatory...” was the formula then in use, full of faith, with which the poor presented themselves.

The appeal to charity was made not so much in the name of poverty as in the name of God, present in the poor.

And Rosa would come out and offer them cooked pulses with a smile, as was the custom in those days.

Other features of her adolescent religion: a piety based not on emotions but on convictions, and her openness to everyone, even to those far from the faith.

Here is a particularly modern side of her personality. One might say that in her attitude to those far away Rosa Gattorno anticipated the Council.

In the Second Vatican Council’s Constitution on the Church in the Modern World we read: “The Church... while rejecting atheism root and branch, sincerely professes that all men, believers and unbelievers alike, ought to work for the rightful betterment of this world in which all alike live; such an ideal cannot be realized, however, apart from sincere and prudent dialogue.”

The “unbelievers” Rosa had to deal with were followers of Mazzini and Garibaldi, who often met at the Gattorno house.

Rosa knew how to hold her own with these gentlemen. Her speech was clear, simple and cordial.

“Rosa,” her brother Francesco testifies, “never gave way where ideas were concerned.”

Immovable on principles, flexible in understanding, kindness and friendship: a “sincere and prudent” dialogue, as the Council asks.

A dialogue that inspires trust and liking. And liking for a Christian is already something: it is the first step towards the ideas embodied in the Christian.

Few people in the world live this threefold experience: wife, mother, religious.

Rosa Gattorno was fiancée, wife and mother.

This range of experience would give her figure as foundress an extraordinary fullness of humanity. With her Sisters she would always be a mother rather than a Superior.

Her tender love for her children she would transfer to her spiritual daughters. “To go to God because one has fallen out of love with the earth and sorrow has cut us off from the world is useless. God needs souls attached to the world. It is in our joy that he delights” (A. Camus).

To choose God is not to renounce the world and its values; rather, it is to love them all the more. God has no use for disappointed, disenchanted, frustrated, sad souls. He wants souls in love in his service.

The Lamba-Doria palace, where the Gattorno family lived, was much frequented by young men of good family who came on business or for political conversation.

Rosa’s presence — a girl who joined good looks to mature judgment and a gentle character — soon won over the young visitors. Proposals of marriage were not long in coming.

Rosa would have been ready to accept the proposal of a cousin, Gerolamo Custo: honest, comfortably off — she felt she loved him.

But her father put forward another name: the lawyer Tito Orsini, an able jurist of the Genoa bar, brother of a famous follower of Mazzini, Angelo Orsini, who had been taken prisoner in the revolutionary risings of 1833.

Orsini appealed to her father for his intelligence and brilliant position, but he disappointed everyone by his unstable character and his conduct.

Signor Gattorno would no longer receive him in his house.

Then her cousin Gerolamo Custo came forward and was welcomed by all.

Rosa prepared for the great step by praying and listening to the advice of her new spiritual director, Fr Antonio Accinelli, for she had had some doubts about her vocation.

“Father, is this really my path?”

“It is true that you have certain inclinations that might seem to show the signs of a religious vocation. You love prayer, you like being with the nuns, you love the poor and the sick. But all that is not enough. Is it true or not that you also love Gerolamo?”

“Yes.”

“And isn’t Gerolamo a good young man who gives you every chance of founding a truly Christian family?”

“Certainly.”

“Then go ahead in peace...”

Added to this was her parents’ express wish, which for Rosa was like a command.

The ecclesiastical dispensations for consanguinity were requested, and on 5 November 1852 Rosa and Gerolamo were married.

As was the custom in many families of the time, the wedding was celebrated in the Gattorno house. The next morning the couple received the nuptial blessing in the cathedral of San Lorenzo, since some months earlier the Gattorno family had moved to a house in that parish. The blessing was given by Fr Antonio Accinelli, the cathedral’s curate.

Is not life, in any state, a sacrifice?

It is told of St Frances of Rome that she bowed to marriage at her father’s wish after a memorable conversation with the Benedictine monk Dom Antonio.

“Is not life,” the monk had said to her, “in any state, a sacrifice?”

Her sister Elisa noticed that during the wedding celebrations Rosa did not show the joy brides usually show on such occasions.

“She bore herself modestly and was cheerful without letting herself be carried away by joy.”

Did she perhaps foresee the destiny of sorrow that awaited her?

The honeymoon was short-lived.

“On the very evening of the wedding the couple left Genoa for Marseilles, where Gerolamo had his business. There Signor Custo soon discovered the disastrous state of his affairs. A few days of anxiety on the brink of the opening abyss. Anguished silence... in the torture of the inevitable, together with a thread of hope, or rather of illusion.

“In the end the secret was useless and impossible to keep.

It was financial ruin! In a few months, from opulent wealth to poverty: this was what he had to reveal to his young wife. Rosa’s dismay is easy to imagine. She at once appealed to her father, who hurried from Genoa and, skilled as he was in business, managed to salvage a little from the wreck. But Custo’s future in Marseilles was finished for ever. Signor Francesco had to bring his daughter and son-in-law back to Genoa and take them into his house, for Alessandro Custo, Rosa’s father-in-law, was not a man to open his arms to those poor castaways; indeed, from then on relations between the two families suffered some strain.”

On 8 December 1853, the feast of the Immaculate Conception, Rosa gave birth to a daughter, Carlotta. Around the baby’s cradle the Gattorno and Custo families renewed their bonds of friendship.

But soon there came a new trial. Carlotta fell ill. Violent spasmodic convulsions racked the little body. Within a few weeks she lost her hearing and her voice died away. Deaf and dumb. For ever.

Two years later came her second motherhood. In the villa at Sampierdarena, on 28 October 1855, Alessandro was born.

Their finances improved. The Custos moved house and settled in the parish of S. Siro, still in Genoa.

But Rosa continued to attend the Metropolitan Cathedral of San Lorenzo.

There she found a new spiritual director, Fr Giuseppe Firpo, who would guide her until she left Genoa.3

What matters in the spiritual life is to find a master.

“How do you draw such marvellous statues out of a block of marble?” they once asked Michelangelo.

“It’s all in the marble,” the famous sculptor replied. “You just have to know how to strike it.”

The world is full of saints who never were. There was no master to strike, to forge, to point out the goals of holiness.

Young people are always ready.

In every young person there is a hero or a saint waiting to be awakened.

Fr Firpo believed in the potential of the young.

To the young spiritual daughter who had entrusted herself to him he at once pointed out lofty goals and set out a total program: the Gospel sine glossa, Christian through and through, not sweetened.

Weekly Confession and Communion — something very few practiced then. Fidelity to the duties of one’s state.

Her husband was violent and harsh: overcome anger with gentleness. The secret of everything: prayer.

“At night she would withdraw to pray to God for strength in her trials.”

“It may be punishment, it may be mercy”

Before the suffering of the plague victims and the suffering of Don Rodrigo, Manzoni comes out with this phrase: “It may be punishment, it may be mercy.”

The mystery of suffering, the mystery of Calvary.

Rosa now faced another stage of her Calvary: her husband’s departure for Russia. He had gone into partnership with his brother-in-law Federico Gattorno, who had opened a trading house in the city of Berdjanaka, and he had to leave.

So towards the end of 1855 Rosa was left alone, for more than a year, wholly taken up with caring for the two children.

In Russia Gerolamo’s business prospered, but his health declined. At the beginning of 1857 he had to return to Genoa, arriving in a very poor state.

The illness soon proved serious and incurable: pulmonary tuberculosis.

While her husband was ill, their third child, Francesco, was born.

Three small children, one of them deaf and dumb, a household to run, a sick husband. But Rosa’s charity and patience never failed.

“Love hopes all things, endures all things, is patient...” (1 Cor 13:4).

In the last year of his illness she was constantly at her husband’s side, day and night, without even undressing. The priest who some years later drew up Signor Gerolamo’s death certificate felt moved to add these words: “It should be noted that throughout his long illness he was constantly cared for by his wife with charity.”

Charity for the body and charity for the spirit.

“Gerolamo, shall we say the rosary together?”

“Gladly... you lead, so I’ll tire less.”

“Gerolamo, would you like me to read you a few pages of a religious book?”

“Thank you...”

And her husband listened with real devotion to those pages, which detached his spirit more and more from earthly things and anchored it in heavenly ones.4

On 9 March 1858 Gerolamo died.

A few days after her husband’s death Rosa took her three little children to church, to an altar of Our Lady of Sorrows, and in tears offered them, entrusting them to the divine Mother.

“Pray, pray hard,” her spiritual director insisted. “Prayer is strength, love, holiness.”

What a man says in prayer is magic

“A man,” writes Julien Green, “is in danger when he prays; he is in danger even if he prays absent-mindedly, for there are words that cannot be spoken in vain. He prays as though he prayed in vain, but nothing is vain except the idea we form of heaven. What a man says in prayer is magic.”

Strength Rosa truly needed. Other trials awaited her.

Her husband’s coffin was not yet closed when a disgraceful quarrel over the inheritance broke out between the Custo and Gattorno families. The bailiff had to come and seize all the furniture and household goods, including the widow’s bridal trousseau.

Rosa was forced to squeeze into a few rooms furnished with bare necessities. For some nights she had to sleep on a plain straw mattress.

Barely three months after her husband’s death her youngest child, only seven months old, died too. “He was the last flower of her motherhood, born as her husband’s life was waning, and so his most living memory. Death cut him down inexorably. Her grief was such that, as she later confessed, she thought she would go mad. Her confessor, Fr Firpo, had to come several times to comfort her, and in the end he resorted to a strict command of obedience to make her take up her occupations again with courage and care for the two little orphans.”

Her father, Francesco Gattorno, realized that his daughter’s life in such conditions was unbearable and took the widow and children back into his house.

Rosa returned to the rooms of her girlhood. She had left them in a bridal veil; now she came back in a mourning veil with two children at her side.

Her life seemed broken for ever.

But, says the Bible, there is hope for a tree.

From the felled tree a shoot may spring.

God writes straight with crooked lines.

God is a shepherd. Suffering is his dog. Its bite is hard, but it is for our good.

The greatest good the bite of suffering did Rosa Gattorno was to make her see God.

“Judaism,” Chesterton wrote, “in its dark and sublime way, laid down that if a man saw God he would die. Christianity holds (with a fatality even more catastrophic) that if he sees God he will live for ever. In either case what happens will be decisive and beyond all doubt. After seeing God a man may die; but he will certainly not feel slightly unwell, so as to have to take a medicine or call the doctor.”

God had now invaded every path of Rosa’s heart.

When you have God within you, you will have a guest who will never leave you in peace. From this moment Rosa’s spiritual ascent knew no more pauses. She did not run to the doctor; she ran to her brothers and sisters.

She had understood that to love God means to love one’s neighbor.

God is relatively easy to love — or to think we love. We invent him, imagine him, fine-tune him. We draw him near (when we are in a bad mood) and push him away (when we feel fine); we alter his features at will according to our “inspirations”. And in the end he looks like us! Voltaire said: “God created man in his own image and likeness — and man has returned the compliment!” That old egoist Chateaubriand, who never bothered about his wife, called God “the eternal bachelor of the worlds”. One need not look far for the model he had in mind.

“If you tell me, ‘I love God’,” writes Louis Evely, “I hold back; I hesitate to canonize you. It may be a flash in the pan, a pious fancy! But if you tell me, ‘I love my neighbors’, I begin to take notice: here is an extraordinary person. Here at last, perhaps, is someone God can put up with! Do I love God in his heaven? I love nothing but a construction of my imagination. It would be too easy to ‘work out one’s salvation’, to ‘earn heaven’, by setting foot for half an hour a week in a church ‘where, fortunately, one knows nobody’. The only one fed on the flesh of Christ, the only one naturalized ‘heavenly’, is the one who swallows all his brothers along with the Host.”

Rosa, free of the marriage bond, devoted herself entirely to good works. As she contemplated the Crucified naked on the Cross, the desire to be conformed to him grew ever stronger in her heart. To love means to imitate.

“Where material goods are concerned, all that we have more than he did only shows how different we are from him” (Charles de Foucauld).

She visited the poor in their homes and helped them as she could, bringing money, food and clothes. And she gave everything with such affection and tact that the poor were moved. Rosa knew that the poor man is not a vessel to be filled but a reality to be understood and a creature to be loved.

If poverty were only “a lack of things”, it would be enough to fill the gap.

No bread? I’ll stuff you with bread. No clothes? I’ll dress you like a tailor’s dummy.

No: the poor man asks to be loved, as each of us asks to be loved.

How often charity becomes an excuse for washing our hands of justice!

In the name of a supernatural charity we refuse concrete solidarity: I am the one who must do it.

And we forget the truth that the poor man is Christ: not a stranger or an acquaintance, a friend or an enemy, someone near or far, white or black — he is my brother.

“A new commandment I give you: love one another as I have loved you” (Jn 13:34).

And before these words Jesus set about washing their feet.

If we do not go beyond the limits of philanthropy we shall never wash our brothers’ feet: we shall invent social services for foot-washing and pay the foot-washers.

In her father’s house Rosa was given a set of rooms with its own entrance, so that she could go out even at night without her family noticing.

When someone was seriously ill, she would go out at night while the children slept, with one of the maids who was utterly devoted to her, to nurse them.

She visited the sick in hospital, especially those who were alone and poor. She served meals, handed out medicines and made the beds. When she could, she kissed their sores. “For me,” she writes, “when I managed to do that, it was a real comfort.”5

One recalls the episode told by Fr Agostino Gemelli:

“When I was a socialist, anticlerical doctor, the hospital director put me in charge of a small ward of soldiers with leprosy.

“I felt very sorry for those poor lads. I grew particularly fond of them and did all I could to ease their sufferings.

“One evening, as I was crossing the ward, I heard a soldier calling me: ‘Doctor, doctor...’ I went to his bed. ‘Doctor, I know there’s nothing more to be done for me... If I were at home, my mother would give me a kiss before I died... Doctor... will you give me one?’

“My stomach turned at the thought of kissing that face covered with sores. But I made an effort, bent over him and kissed him... Then the soldier said: ‘Now, doctor, do me one more favor: call a priest so that I can make my confession.’”

One day Rosa had no money left to give the poor. She called a servant and asked him to go and sell a gun and a sofa, among the few things saved from seizure after her husband’s death. Her father had hidden them in a storeroom. As soon as he found out he flew into a rage.

“Rosa, it was you who sold the gun and the sofa...”

“Yes...”

“When will you stop these charitable fads of yours? If you go on like this I’ll throw you out of the house.”

The poor woman was already getting ready to leave, silent and humbled, with the two children by the hand. Her father relented, and it all ended in a few reproaches.

O God, send us madmen!

“Let no one deceive himself,” writes St Paul. “If any one among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise” (1 Cor 3:18).

For Fr Lebret, the chief inspirer of the encyclical Populorum Progressio, folly belongs to the theological order and is closely bound to faith, hope and charity. He lamented that today the Christian ranks held too many wise men, too many prudent ones, too many people forever calculating and measuring.

One of his greatest sorrows was to find no folly among Christians, nearly all sick with excessive “prudence”.

To the young people who came asking to join his équipes, Fr Lebret put a simple question:

“Are you mad?”

And he prayed: “O God, send us madmen! We need madmen today...”

Rosa committed follies.

Her follies were modelled on those of Christ Crucified: the folly of the Cross.

For Rosa crosses were an invitation to look ever more at the Cross of Jesus Crucified, to draw inspiration and strength from it. As soon as her husband died she asked to consecrate herself to God by a vow of perpetual chastity; she was allowed to make it for a year. She tied a crucifix seven centimeters high to her breast and kept it pressed there day and night until it sank into her flesh. And when, five years later, she was ordered to remove it, she had to tear it out of the wound it had made, with shreds of tissue.6

Towards the end of 1858, during the novena of the Immaculate Conception, she was allowed to make a perpetual vow of chastity and obedience. She would have liked to vow poverty too, but her wise director, Fr Giuseppe Firpo, did not think it opportune.

Why such hunger for penance?

Because the world needs a mystical balance. Where sin abounds, expiation must abound all the more.

Each of us is responsible for the sins of all.

While Rosa embodied these principles in her own person, in Russia Dostoevsky was scattering them through his novels.

Here are a few gleanings.

“The world is like the ocean: everything flows and everything is connected, so that if you touch it at one point, your touch is felt perhaps at the other end of the earth.

“And for the birds, for the children, for every created being, if you were even a little more faithful than you are now, life would surely be better.

“Everything is like the ocean, I tell you again.”

The Garibaldian’s shirt

The patriot and writer Giuseppe Cesare Abba — so Curatolo tells in his book Aneddoti garibaldini — was asked one day, many years after taking part in the Expedition of the Thousand, by a collector for some object to keep in his museum.

“I have nothing left; only the sabre I carried in 1866, and I have promised to leave it to my children.”

“And the red shirt — do you still have it? Why not give it to me?”

Noticing some embarrassment, the collector apologized:

“Have I troubled you with my question?”

“No, no,” Abba replied.

The next day he sent the collector this letter:

“Dear friend, my red shirt disappeared soon after I came back from Sicily, and I never heard of it again. When my mother died in 1871 I found that she had made two hair shirts out of it and had worn them for ten years. Once she was dead I did not dare take them off her. Abba.”

St Paul has a very strong phrase. He says we have been “conformed to the death of Jesus” (Phil 3:10) in order to share in his glorious resurrection. By baptism we have been grafted into the Mystical Body of Christ. The figure of Christ is the figure of a sufferer; our Head is crowned with thorns. We cannot claim to be unlike him without betraying ourselves.

“The grace of baptism: a grace of martyrdom” (St John Eudes).

“In my flesh I complete what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his Body, that is, the Church” (Col 1:24).

Rosa realized that she was not yet “conformed to the death of Jesus”, that in her flesh she had not yet “completed what is lacking in the passion of Jesus”.

So she asked, and obtained, permission to increase her penances.

“What were her penances? From a document she wrote under obedience we know some of them, which already amount to a formidable torment for nature. From 1856, after the birth of her son Alessandro, when she was 25, she had bound herself by vow to perpetual fasting, taking only one meal a day, always meatless and without wine. She kept to this regime for forty-four years, that is, until her death, admitting no relaxation even in her last illness.

“Every evening she took the discipline until she bled, for the length of two Misereres and De profundis. She put chickpeas in her shoes so that walking would hurt, and she kept this up for eight years, that is, the whole of her widowhood spent in the world. In the country she put nettles against her skin, finding a way to afflict the sense of touch extensively. She also forbade herself heating in winter and, though she suffered greatly from the cold, sometimes to the point of fainting, she allowed no exception for more than eighteen years — until 1876, when, in her forty-fifth year, a pleurisy brought her to death’s door and she had to accept the relief of a little warmth.”

“In 1859 she made herself a leather bodice bristling with iron points; she bound her legs and arms with spiked devices too, and found ways to torment her feet and head. But the most terrible instrument was a chain of thick iron wire with double crossed links, forming a belt about a centimeter thick. She fastened it round her waist and tightened it so that it could no longer be removed. She wore it continuously for more than forty years, until her death. In time the chain sank into her flesh, which became caught here and there in the links, causing the Servant of God great pain; but she did not bring herself to take it off until the eve of her death.”

To adore the Cross and to climb the Cross

Brescia, April 1966. Cardinal Giulio Bevilacqua is dying. To Cardinal Urbani, who has come to visit him, he confides: “I worked hard during Holy Week. All my people came to the various services. How much good this liturgical renewal has done! How many men... how many young people!...”7

Now he was looking at the crucifix and went on, in a faint thread of voice, with his ever pleasant and lively conversation: “It was on Good Friday, during the liturgy, at the adoration of the Cross. I was assisting in my mozzetta and went up to kiss it. Then that fine sentence of Minucius Felix came to mind: ‘It is good to adore the Cross, but now the hour has come to climb onto it and live it!’ I felt that invitation was beautiful, and it seemed meant just for me...”

Rosa too was not content to adore the Cross. She climbed onto it — ever closer, ever more conformed to the Crucified.

During the novena of the Redeemer in 1859 she subjected her body to a stricter fast, spending the vigil on a little bread and a sip of water. “And yet,” she noted, “I felt my strength gradually increasing, as if those penances and the discipline to the point of blood were my greatest nourishment.”

In that same year, 1859, she obtained permission to wear a crown of thorns on her head every Thursday night into Friday.89

“In 1861 she fulfilled a long-cherished dream. Having obtained from the Franciscan friars a length of the cloth they used for their habits, she sewed herself a sleeveless one and wore it under her lay clothes, which, as was the fashion then, were full enough to allow it. She girded it with a thick cord from which a skull hung at one side.

“She wore this habit day and night. Anyone can imagine with what discomfort, especially given its weight and the other instruments of penance she wore.”

She would have liked to do even more, but her spiritual director would not allow it.

“I am very glad you have been able to receive Communion every day.

“... When I think of the great benefits Holy Communion has brought you, I have every reason to tell you that the Lord loves you. Believe me, since you have been receiving it often you have become a different person. Now you belong wholly to Jesus. As for the second part of your letter, I tell you to limit yourself for now to the mortifications I have allowed you.”

What are we to say of these penances?

“Pious inventions of the biographers,” some will protest.

Impossible. There is reliable testimony. In two rooms, in Rome and in Piacenza, all these instruments used by the Servant of God are still on display today.

“Eccentricities, medieval stuff,” others will maintain. “They mustn’t be taken too seriously. We all have our quirks, after all!”

“Masochism!” the more intellectual will confidently suggest, eyeing with suspicion all the bodily mortifications of the saints of every age and treating them as products suspect under scientific analysis.10

Agreed: the essence of holiness does not lie in sleeping on planks, fasting and making one’s skin bleed, but in the capacity to fling one’s soul and heart towards the stars.

Agreed: bodily mortifications are not always the most important. An episode in the Vitae Patrum is telling in this regard:

“Epiphanius, Bishop of Cyprus, once sent this message to Abbot Hilarion: ‘Come down to me, that we may know each other before we leave the body.’ When they were seated together at table, some fowl was brought in, and the Bishop set it before Hilarion. At once the old man said: ‘Forgive me, father; since I put on the monastic habit I have not dared to eat meat that was killed.’ The Bishop replied: ‘And I, since I have worn the episcopal insignia, have never let anyone go to bed with a grudge against me, nor have I ever been able to fall asleep without first being reconciled with anyone who had opposed me.’ Then the old man said: ‘Forgive me, father: you have gone much further on the way of life than I.’”

Agreed. The devil too — so an old saying goes — neither eats, drinks nor marries, and yet that supreme ascetic is, formally, no less a devil for it...

Agreed on all this.

The fact remains, however, that mortification cannot vanish from Christian life with impunity; the price is its inevitable slide into comfortable mediocrity.

It will do no harm to rediscover the meaning and dynamism of the asceticism practiced by early monasticism. Let me quote some passages from an acute analysis by a specialist:

“It would be an unforgivable mistake to see in the desert only the dregs of monasticism, uncultured men living in a degrading atmosphere. Unless one goes down to the deep motives, one risks passing by a unique fact with incalculable consequences for the destiny of Christianity. The asceticism of the desert is an inescapable dialectical moment of Christian spirituality.

“Not with the tools of culture but with their bare hands the ascetics kept the Christian ideal at its transcendent height. And there lies the miracle.

“Asceticism lessens the effects of the original stain and shows the power of the spirit. The ‘bestiary’ of the desert tells of an astonishing friendship: wild beasts recognized the scent of paradise near the saints and ended by becoming humanized, mirroring the human face with gentle, intelligent eyes. The anchorites relive man’s ancient privilege, set by God as cosmic word and king of the universe.

“It is in the maximalism of the ascetics that the world finds its measure, its point of comparison, and grasps the dangerous insipidity and flatness of every self-satisfied spirit. Against common sense — ‘God does not ask so much’ — asceticism proclaims the terrible jealousy of God who, having given all of himself, asks everything of man. The Desert Fathers leave an icon of this total gift. Their excessive features only catch the eye and put questions to every man about his own ‘possible’.

“Asceticism has purified the soul; it keeps its role of watchful sentinel.

“By placing itself in antisocial conditions, asceticism prepared the return of the new man into history. Placed at its origins outside history, monasticism would become a religious force destined to influence history all the more powerfully.”11

Clearly it is not a matter of returning to the forms of early monastic asceticism, but only to its spirit.

In today’s conditions — and the observation is again Evdokimov’s — with a pace of life ever more dizzying and crushing, causing frightening nervous wear and tear, Christian mortification must necessarily acquire a new sensitivity and adopt new forms.

“Asceticism is only a method at the service of life and must fit new needs. The heroic Thebaid imposed extreme fasts. Today the battle has shifted. Man does not need extra pain; hair shirts and scourges would risk breaking him for nothing. Mortification will rather consist in freedom from every need for speed, noise, stimulants, alcohol.

“Asceticism will consist in knowing how to allow oneself due rest, how to stop and find again, in calm and silence, at regular intervals, prayer and contemplation, even amid the din of the world; above all in being aware of the presence of others.

“Fasting, instead of the old macerations, will mean renouncing the superfluous, being able to share bread with the poor, a smiling balance.

“These may be the new forms of asceticism, typical of what has been called ‘interiorized monasticism’.”

“Calvary alone I know to be the sure mountain on which to rest”

In the space of four years Rosa had climbed so high in self-purification and union with Christ that the quick accents of her aspirations bore the stamp of the Cross.

“The suffering grew, and I thanked my Beloved who provided me with such sweet food.”

“O love! You who suffered so much for me, grant that I may suffer for you and die for you.”

“Calvary alone I know to be the sure mountain on which to rest.”

She went through periods of exhaustion, emaciation and illness. But Fr Firpo still granted her all the penances she asked for, because he had found that when he forbade them her health grew worse.

Towards the end of 1869 [?], on the feast of the Immaculate Conception, Rosa also made the vow of poverty.

Beneath her secular clothes she was already a soul wholly consecrated to the Lord.

On the very day of the last vow she wrote:

“Most Holy Mary, teach me to overcome every least trace of human respect and to reach the highest perfection.”

12

“The golden mean according to Christ lies terribly at an extreme” (Régamey).

Rosa stands in the golden mean precisely because she is at the extreme of penance, of prayer, of a life of intense union with God, and at the same time of complete self-giving to her neighbor through charity.

She was involved in a great many charitable institutions and always ready to respond to appeals for help.

All this without neglecting the care she owed first of all to her children. Carlotta, the deaf-mute, grew up innocent and pure, but because of her disability she could not benefit much from her mother’s teaching. So her mother decided to place her in the Royal Institute for the Deaf and Dumb in Milan. She took her there and stayed with her until she saw her settled.

Alessandro grew up lively, intelligent, very sensitive and devout. At nine he said: “When I grow up I’ll be a priest.”

In the autumn of 1864 it was decided to send him to the preparatory school for ecclesiastical studies at Carignano.

Four years later the boy entered the seminary at Savona run by the Vincentian Fathers. But he did not persevere. His youth would go astray. […]
