“Where the devil do you hide your joy?”

The more her penances increased, the more her joy grew. Those who met Rosa Gattorno were astonished to find her always serene and smiling.

Rosa certainly did not deserve the reproach Bernanos puts in the mouth of an unbeliever: “We cannot see into your consciences,” he says to a believer, “but we study with more interest and imagination the vocabulary you use without understanding any longer, from overuse, its inner meaning. Does it not contain, above all, this mysterious expression: ‘the state of grace’? When you come out of the confessional you are in ‘the state of grace’. The state of grace... And yet, you see, it hardly shows. We wonder what you do with the grace of God. Shouldn’t it shine on your faces? Where the devil do you hide your joy?”

Rosa, on the contrary, would tell her daughters: “Being able to do something pleasing to God is enough for me to find every kind of happiness in suffering.”

And again: “Be cheerful, my daughters, be cheerful; Jesus loves those who suffer. Whoever will not suffer will not love.”

Yet she would not be spared those terrible trials that mystical theology calls “passive purifications” and that St John of the Cross calls the “dark night”, distinguishing it from the “night of sense”, the loss of sensible consolations: the “dark night” is the night of the spirit, which unleashes in the soul a mass of desolation, doubt and bitterness.131415

This twofold night descended on Rosa’s soul so that her virtue might be ever more refined.

Fr Fiocchi copies from the Memoirs: “Once again under the heaviest trials one could name. Patience! How beautiful it is to suffer for love of Jesus, deprived of all consolation.”

A few months later she prayed:

“Press upon my breast, O Jesus, the dear standard of the Cross; but measure my strength, so that I may carry it well and climb the mount of sorrow, Calvary, and, victorious, ever close to you, die there crucified with you.”

To dryness were added other pains: scruples and doubts about her past confessions. And Fr Firpo, firm and energetic, forbade her in the most categorical terms to repeat her general confession.

Fr Firpo, however, was becoming ever more convinced that he was dealing with a soul guided by higher lights, in whom God was acting in a singular way. So in 1864, after six months of experience and careful examination, he wrote telling her to abandon herself entirely to the inner spirit guiding her.

“As for the accounts you give me of your spirit, I will tell you this: how incomprehensible are the judgments of God, and by how many ways he draws souls! It is no longer you who live. It is your Spouse Jesus, your love, your all, who lives and works in you. If, then, you are dead and live no longer, let him who lives in you dispose of everything. In his lofty and loving designs you must serve him only as a wretched instrument, which is what you are.”1617

Truth is born only of the truth of persons

A saint is like a magnet: he draws people to himself.

“When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (Jn 12:32).

People of God have no need to speak; it is enough that they exist. Their presence is already a call. “To fight error means first of all to overcome it in oneself. Even if the Church alone holds the deposit of truth, truth is born only of the truth of persons, as faith of faith and love of love” (Jean Sulivan).

At this point in Rosa Gattorno’s life we witness a fascination, a radiance explicable only by the power of witness. Around her gathered an ever more varied circle of people — devout, indifferent, unbelieving. What drew them?

“They see that woman so battered by events, so lashed by human selfishness, so frighteningly alone in her young widowhood before her children’s future,” and yet always strong, serene and smiling.

Many Genoese ladies sought Rosa’s friendship and asked to share in her apostolate — among them Giulia Galleri, Adele Bensa, Countess Carolina Gavotti, Marchioness Isabella Lamba Doria, Marchioness Emilia Negrone and Teresa Morasso.

They not only worked with her but entrusted themselves to her for help and support on their spiritual journey.

A cousin of the same name wrote to her: “Among the many benefits I have received from God, unworthy as I am, I count this too: having your friendship, for it is a truly good friendship, aimed at the good of my poor soul... Yes, you are right: your reproaches are only too just, and your advice more than salutary and timely...”18

Wherever a saint passes, something is always born. Truth does not need to be told. It is enough that it be lived.

Gandhi puts it well:

“It is better to let our lives speak for us than our words. God did not bear the Cross only nineteen hundred years ago; he bears it today, and dies and rises day by day. It would be poor comfort to the world if it had to depend on a historical God who died two thousand years ago. Do not preach the God of history, then; show him as he lives in you today.

“I do not believe in people telling others of their faith chiefly in order to convert. Faith does not admit of telling. It has to be lived, and then it spreads of itself.”

The letters of Rosa’s friends often turn to the theme of charity.

“I cannot tell you,” writes Signora Giulia Galleri, “how pleased I was that you let me share in the service of holy charity these past days. It is a fresh proof of your kindness, for which I shall always be grateful. Your poor old ladies send you a thousand blessings and long to see their great benefactress soon.”192021

And in another letter: “What is more beautiful and holy than the sacrifice of a soul who, setting aside every thought of this world, consecrates herself to the service of the suffering, regarding all people as brothers in the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus?” This shows that in the school of her friend Rosa, Signora Galleri had learned the center, the heart of Christian spirituality: love of neighbor... the poor, the old and the suffering seen with the eyes of faith, “as brothers of Jesus”.

When one has chosen the poor, one can be sure one has not gone wrong. When one has chosen an ideology, one can never be sure of having taken the best side. But when one has chosen the poor, one is always sure — doubly sure — of having made a good choice.

All the letters of Rosa’s friends are dominated by charity: girls at risk to be placed, poor people to be helped, meetings for pious works, preparations for religious feasts, the founding of charitable institutions for orphans and the destitute of every kind.

“Charity does not begin at home but wherever unhappiness first shows itself. Charity does not consist in handing over pain and loneliness to the police. Charity is made of emery paper on one side and cotton wool on the other” (Bruce Marshall).

“We possess only what we give... We possess ourselves only when we give ourselves” (Emmanuel Mounier).

I take this dialogue from a book by Baunard:

“Sir, don’t read good books...”

“What?”

“No — read only the excellent ones, the best.”

“Contact with genius gives us an immediate benefit: it raises us. Even before they teach us anything, their superiority is already a gift. Then they set the tone. They accustom us to the heights” (Sertillanges).

Books shoot further than cannons. The [great] revolutions, from the Christian to the Muslim, [from the] French to the Communist, are kindled and [fed] by a book. Rosa Gattorno shows an extraordinary modernity in her love of books too. [As a] young woman she had not been very familiar with [books]. But later she would show her faith in the book as an instrument of the apostolate — like [Don] Bosco, who spread books and [founded] libraries wherever he went.

In those years, between 1855 and 1860, the “Pious Association in honor of Mary Immaculate for the preservation and growth of the Catholic [Faith]” was active in Genoa. It had been founded by Fr Giuseppe Frassinetti. At first it consisted only of men, who worked especially to spread good books. But it soon had a women’s section and brought various works of zeal under a common direction. The women’s section met in the oratory of St Ambrose, sometimes honored by the presence of the Archbishop of Genoa, Mgr Charvaz, under whom it came directly.

Rosa Gattorno joined. She attended the meetings regularly and busied herself circulating books.

She was convinced that a book can be a vehicle of grace. As the author of the Imitation of Christ wrote: “Take a book into your hands as Simeon the Just took the Child Jesus into his arms to hold him and kiss him.”

Another association active in Genoa at that time was the “Pious Union of the Daughters of Mary Most Holy Immaculate”, also founded by Frassinetti. Unmarried women were preferred, but young widows of good will, resolved to remain continent, were also accepted. Their spirit was: practice of the evangelical counsels, much prayer, daily Communion, apostolate in the family and in the world.

By 1864 Rosa Gattorno was one of its best-formed and most active members.

The Archbishop of Genoa made her president. In 1865 a Commission for girls at risk was set up in Genoa, and Rosa was elected vice-president.

This work for girls at risk had always been her dream.

Rosa feared the “ghetto”. The temptation of the ghetto always lies in wait on the Christian’s path. It is so pleasant to be among ourselves: the same language, the warmth of friendship.

The Gospel, on the contrary, means “going” — going to those far away, to sinners.

Girls at risk were mission territory. Rosa set to work at once. She raised funds, looked for helpers and sought out, in the city and the countryside, young women exposed to particular moral dangers or already enslaved by evil.

Meanwhile an idea was taking shape in her mind: why not gather her helpers into an institution to care for these girls?

Among the Daughters of Mary, of whom she was president, there were truly well-formed, generous women ready to be launched into an apostolic enterprise. “Father,” she said to her spiritual director, Fr Firpo, “I would like to tell you of a plan I have long cherished: to gather some Daughters of Mary and live in community under a rule suited to our circumstances.”

“I can only approve the plan.”

Fr Firpo was by now convinced that his spiritual daughter was truly the object of extraordinary graces.

“You have spoken to me,” he wrote on 18 March 1864, “of the Daughters of Mary whom you hope to make Ursulines: if that happens, it means that this too was in the designs of Divine Providence.”

In the various Pious Unions where she worked she picked out some women, the most devout and zealous. “You will be the leaven that makes our Union rise.”

They were called Ursulines, a name commonly used in Genoa for women living in the world under a rule of religious life.

They formed a small religious family of their own, with their own meetings and common rules of spiritual life.22

Rosa was their Superior.

The church authorities were kept informed. They watched over the experiment for a whole year, after which Mgr Charvaz officially approved the infant congregation and appointed Rosa Gattorno its first Superior.

Almost without realizing it, guided by Providence, Rosa had laid the first foundations of a new congregation.

Canon Guido Botto would be its spiritual director.

“So now you are a Superior... You will share with St Jane de Chantal and St Teresa the office of director of souls,” her friend Marchioness Lamba-Doria wrote from Paris.

Guess what displeases me

“Signora Rosa, could you do me a favor...?”

“Gladly, if I can...”

And Fr Frassinetti explained the matter. He had prepared a new version of the rules for the Daughters of Mary and presented it to the Archbishop, but the Archbishop was reluctant to approve it.

“You, who enjoy such esteem and influence with the Archbishop, couldn’t you put in a word?”

Rosa went to the Archbishop with a copy of the rules.

“I know them already, but I don’t feel I can approve them unless some changes are made. And I don’t know whether Fr Frassinetti is willing to make them.”

“Your Excellency, I think he is...”23

“In any case, I want you to guess what displeases me in these rules.”

Rosa was astonished and silent.

“Go, and come back when you have made your notes.”

And he ended the interview.

That night, clasping her crucifix, Rosa prayed for a long time.

Prayer is light. Rosa soon discovered the points that were wrong and noted them down.

The next day she went to Fr Frassinetti: “Don Giuseppe, Monsignor is willing to approve the rules if you remove a few points.”

And she pointed them out.

The man of God had no difficulty in accepting what the Archbishop wanted.

And so the rules were approved.

A light in the night

Mortification has a bad press today. It looks like a relic of the Middle Ages. To certain over-advanced progressives penance seems so much cumbersome junk. But is that really right?

Let us open the Gospel. Christ told us not to look gloomy when we fast; so he did not exclude fasting. Here are his words: “When you fast, do not look dismal, like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces that their fasting may be seen by men. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, that your fasting may not be seen by men but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you” (Mt 6:16-18).

From February 1863 to February 1864 Rosa Gattorno, with her spiritual director’s permission, kept a very strict fast. For twelve months she took no food or drink except four ounces of bread every twenty-four hours and a sip of water. And she ate that little food over a skull at one in the morning.

Yet she never lacked the strength to carry out her duties.

Did she perhaps feel in her heart that she needed special graces?

Did she sense that God was about to call her to an important task in the Church?

Indeed, as she held her crucifix to her breast after correcting Fr Frassinetti’s rules and gave thanks for the light received, her mind was seized by a very clear idea of another rule, for a new congregation that might be founded.

She at once wrote down her thoughts, folded the sheet, put it in a safe place and went on praying.

The more she prayed, the more insistent the call became.

She did not hide from herself the difficulties of this vocation. Founding a congregation meant leaving her children and leaving her parents, to whom she was bound by the tenderest affection.

“My God, I feel my strength is not equal to what you ask of me... I haven’t the courage, I can’t...”

At last she decided to speak of it, in confidence, to Fr Firpo, her confessor.

“Why have you hesitated and delayed so long? Put everything before the Archbishop at once.”

Rosa wrote down how the idea had come to her, added a first draft of the Rules and presented it all to Mgr Charvaz.

The Archbishop read it and sent for her. “I cannot describe,” she relates, “my confusion. I was trembling like a leaf. I was so agitated that when I reached his feet I could not speak at all.”

“Obey the Lord’s inspirations. The work you found will be very beautiful.”

“Does the Rule I have written seem right to you?”

“In substance, yes. It will need a little retouching. And then an internal rule of life will have to be drawn up.”

A few days later the Archbishop sent for her again:

“I have asked Mgr Magnasco, the cathedral penitentiary, to help you draw up the rule of life.”

But the rule of life prepared by Mgr Magnasco did not please the Archbishop and was not approved.

“Do you like this rule of life?” he asked Rosa Gattorno.

“Frankly, no. Indeed some points do not seem to me in keeping with the plan I presented.”

“I don’t like them either,” the Archbishop replied. “Then mark the passages you disapprove of with your fingernail. That way Mgr Magnasco won’t notice the correction.”

A few days later the booklet, duly amended by Rosa, was back on the Archbishop’s desk.

Some months passed, and Rosa was again summoned by the Archbishop.

“Mgr Magnasco’s rule of life needs too many corrections... You draw up a new one.”

Rosa understood what the Archbishop was aiming at. He wanted her to leave everything and everyone to found a new congregation.

“Not that,” Rosa kept saying, “never; I [cannot] leave them.”

The Archbishop insisted.

“If you really insist, let me first consult the Pope.”

A day I shall never forget

The ship sails calmly on. The Mediterranean between Genoa and Livorno is as smooth as a mirror of oil.

Suddenly a violent jolt alarms the whole crew.

Are they sinking?

Only one of the steamer’s paddle wheels had broken. Great panic, but no one dead or injured.

Rosa faints from fright.

“Would you like some coffee?”

But there is no persuading her to take even a sip of water. She wants to receive Communion in Livorno.

On New Year’s Day 1866 she arrived in Rome with a bundle of letters of recommendation in her pocket.

Her audience was set for 3 January at two in the afternoon.

“This day,” the Servant of God would write, “I shall never forget.”

She was shown in and knelt at the feet of Pius IX, who blessed her like a father and made her rise at once.

“My daughter, I have read your Rule. It is truly beautiful. What are you waiting for to put it into practice?”

“Holy Father, my parents are old and I have two children still young who need my care.”

“No matter, no matter,” Pope Mastai replied. “God wills it so.”

“But according to the Gospel God will call me to account for my children. I love them too much. I cannot leave them. Impossible.”

Tears choked her. She could not go on.

“If you do not do what God wants of you,” the Pope warned, “you will feel remorse and never have peace again for the rest of your life.”

The Gospel has claws that end up tearing through the gloves

A German atheist writes: “No word of the Gospel lives for itself: it waits for a circumstance, an event, an encounter; then you realize that it was spoken for you and you for it. It grips you, crushes you, tortures you, seems new to you. It is no longer part of the written world. It enters the blood. You no longer master it... All that remains is to set the dogs within us on it... to strangle it... or to listen to it and live it...”

Cardinal Bevilacqua comments: “You cannot put gloves on the Gospel. Nobody could, anyway. The Gospel has claws that end up tearing through the gloves.”

For Rosa Gattorno the Pope’s word was the word of Jesus, because in the Pope she saw “sweet Christ on earth”.

His last words floored her, crushed her, tortured her.

She could not set the dogs of her uncertainty on those words. They had already torn through the gloves of her fear.24

“Holy Father,” she replied, “I want to do God’s will.”

From this “Fiat” the new Institute would be born, to be called the “Daughters of Saint Anne”.

Pius IX added: “This Institute will spread rapidly, like the flight of a dove, to every part of the world. God will take care of your children; you take care of God in his Work.”

He invited her to come to his desk, gave her two photographs of himself with a few words of dedication and meanwhile comforted her like a father.

“Your father and mother will become reconciled to it. You will lack nothing. Everything will be given you. I’ll keep this rule. No doubt you have another copy. Later you will see to giving it the form of a rule of life.”

Rosa stayed in Rome for twenty-eight days.

Bishops and cardinals loaded her with gifts for the chapel of the first house she would open.

But the greatest gift was a document in Pius IX’s own hand authorizing her to reserve the Blessed Sacrament in [her house]. […]

When Rosa announced at home that she was leaving to start a new congregation, all hell broke loose. Father, mother, brothers and sisters were all weep[ing] and begging her not to go. But in some cases it is mercy to show no mercy. “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.”

Her mother, determined to prevent her daughter’s departure at all costs, sat down on the threshold, saying amid tears and dismay: “We’ll see if [you] have the courage to step over me.”25

A real barrier of love was trying to block a higher love.

But time was pressing. Her companions were already at the station; the train left at ten. Then a flash of grace crossed Rosa’s mind. She turned suddenly towards the door, leapt over her mother and found herself on the landing. She ran down the stairs and set off for the station.

The train she had boarded was the Genoa–Piacenza. The Lord had arranged that the cradle of the new congregation should be Piacenza, not Genoa — through a chance meeting in Rome (but nothing is chance; all is Providence).

Where she was staying in Rome, Rosa had met a priest from Piacenza, Fr Luigi Cogrossi.

“Stop for a while in Piacenza,” Fr Cogrossi told her.

Tired on her journey back from Rome, Rosa agreed. She stopped in Piacenza and stayed at a hotel. There she met two “priests of excellent spirit”, the brothers Canons Chiappino, who went out of their way to help her.

They spoke to the Vicar General and to Bishop Ranza and at once found a little house. All that remained was to go. And what would Mgr Charvaz say? “Then let’s set to work,” he exclaimed when he heard the outcome of the meeting with the Pope.

“But not in Genoa, Your Excellency — in Piacenza.” Astonishment, surprise, disappointment. He had already dreamed of a new hearth of light and charity in his own diocese!...

Later, however, he accepted what he too regarded as God’s will.

“But you remain president of the Congregations...!”

“[…] you command me...”

Rosa was now at peace. She was leaving with her Archbishop’s blessing. Twelfth of March 1866.

I was sick and you visited me...

Sampierdarena, Pontedecimo...

As the train puffs and toils up the slopes of the Apennines, in a small compartment the first nucleus of the new Institute reads, prays and chats in friendship.

There are seven of them: Teresa Porta, widow Morasso, Rosa’s close friend; Giovanna Bixio, widow Marchi; Angiola Degrossi of Genoa; Anna Grasso of Pontedecimo; Luigia Rocca, widow Ferro, of Genoa; Amalia Custo; and Rosa.

They reached Piacenza in the afternoon and at once took possession of the very modest rented rooms — perhaps, though it is not certain, at 34 bis Strada della Morte.

They called themselves “Daughters of the Immaculate and Minims of St Francis”.

They divided their time between prayer and visiting the sick.

Rooms, clothes, food — everything breathed genuine, evangelical poverty.

Lavishness only towards the sick.

“Who are those two ladies?” the [teacher] Onorata Colli asked a friend.

“They’re two ‘Genoese ladies’” (that was what the people of Piacenza first called Rosa’s companions).

“What are they going to do in that attic?”

“Up there the wife of a poor day-lab[ourer], one Carlo Cella, is ill. He’s the only one working; [you] can [imagine] what he earns at his trade, and […]

Within a few months a fine group of postulants filled the gaps left by the first desertions.

“To work,” Rosa would say. “There will be no lack of crosses, but there will be no lack of Providence either.”

The gift of Saint Anne

Prayer and sacrifice are the foundations of the new building.

The first draft of the Rules asked the postulants for three hours of prayer after rising at five, another half hour before the midday meal and two hours in the afternoon.

Not just a spirit of poverty, but real poverty. They lived on alms given or begged.

Their main occupation, the purpose the Institute set out to fulfill: nursing the sick poor in their homes.

Eighth of December 1866, feast of the Immaculate Conception: the clothing of the first novices. A dramatic turn: Rosa Gattorno’s companions changed their name and became the “Daughters of Saint Anne”. Why?

Fr Giovanni Battista Tornatore, a Vincentian missionary and professor at the Alberoni College in Piacenza, had recently entered their story. As learned as he was holy, he cherished the wish that a religious family of “Daughters of the Immaculate Motherhood of Saint Anne” should arise in the Church — “Daughters of Saint Anne” as the woman in whose womb was conceived, of a man, immaculate, she who would conceive by the Holy Spirit: Mary of Nazareth, mother of Jesus.

Chosen by Rosa as her confessor, Fr Tornatore shared his ideal with her: “Saint Anne must have a family.” After some hesitation Rosa embraced it, having herself been inspired in prayer, sure that the honor the new family paid to Saint Anne would redound to Mary.

Rosa led the Institute to recognize and love Saint Anne in the figure Fr Tornatore masterfully drew in the Rule of 1869: “In me all the righteousness and all the holiness of the old law were fulfilled; in me rested the groans, the sighs, the tears and the prayers of all the just of the Old Testament, because from me, as from the most fruitful root of Jesse, sprang my Immaculate Daughter and Jesus Christ, her Son and the Son of God, source of the new law of love.”

Daughters of Saint Anne, then. They would not lose Mary Immaculate.

The first clothing ceremony was performed by the Vicar General, Angelo Testa. Rosa, both for family reasons and to protect the Institute, could not receive the veil that day.

“Your community is born,” Mgr Testa wrote to her a few days later, “like the works of the Lord, in darkness: with it and in the midst of it, it must grow. The time of light will come, the time to work at length and openly. For now it is best to work in silence.”

“You are the light of the world...”

“...Let people see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven.”

Around Genoa and Piacenza people began to see the work of these servants of the poor.

And many girls wanted to join them.

In 1867 twenty postulants entered.

It is the Cross that saves

It was with these newcomers that Rosa Gattorno received the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne on 26 July 1867.

She prepared for the great day with much prayer and much penance.

By day she worked and did penance. By night she prayed and did penance.

She chose a small, secluded little room on the mezzanine — very poor, but with the privilege of sharing a wall with the little chapel where Jesus was present in the Blessed Sacrament.

It was reached by a little wooden staircase. No one else was allowed in.

In this cubbyhole she spent some hours of the day and many of the night, praying, meditating, scourging herself.

On the bed a rough straw mattress of maize leaves, with no proper mattress and no blankets.

There she took her brief rest wrapped in a black shawl. Sometimes, removing even the straw mattress, she lay on the iron slats.

More often, her spiritual director says, she liked to lie on a large black cross placed sometimes on the straw mattress, sometimes on the floor.

Her head rested on a thick rough chain coiled into a ball, and round her temples was an iron crown with spikes, like a crown of thorns.

Her hunger to be ever more like her “Spouse” made her find ever new ways of tormenting her body.

Why such love of penance? Rosa Gattorno herself explains:

“Let us not deceive ourselves: in the works of the Lord patience and sacrifice are needed. God likes sacrifices better than great promises or anything else. Jesus sacrificed himself for us, and right to the last evening he drank the bitter cup.”

“Being able to do something pleasing to God is enough for me to find every kind of happiness in suffering.”

“Whoever will not suffer will not love.” “Sorrows turn into joy when one suffers for the Lord.”

A “leader” with a Cross on his shoulders

Rosa truly believed that to love means to imitate. Our Head is crowned with thorns; we, the members, cannot be comfortable and bourgeois.

Wilhelm Munerman tells how Henry II, the holy German emperor, was on his way to do some works of charity with a servant when he got lost in a forest far from the city:

“... They walked for many hours through the thick blanket of snow trying to find the way. The servant, exhausted, began to complain that he could go no further: ‘My lord, I can’t go on. Let me rest a few moments!’

“But Henry, who knew well the danger such a rest would mean in the bitter winter cold, turned to his servant and comforted him: ‘Friend, friend! Follow in my footsteps and it will do you good!’

“The servant obeyed the Emperor’s command and felt an extraordinary warmth and strength rising from the saint’s footprints and filling his whole body. Strengthened in this way, he walked behind the Emperor until, at first light, they found the road that led them out of the snow-covered forest.”26

This urgency of sacrifice proposed by Rosa’s life matches the demands sociologists, psychologists and scientists put to us today.

“The future ‘leader’ who truly captures the imagination of Americans, especially the young, will carry a Cross on his shoulders” (F. Sheen).

Some years ago the poet Lanza del Vasto was asked:

“Why do you protest against war by fasting?”

“Because fasting attacks the source of violence and aggression in man!”

At the clothing, in a public declaration, Rosa restated for herself and her sisters the purpose of the new congregation: “To take in girls at risk so as to keep them from losing their innocence and virtue; to nurse the sick in their homes, night and day, free of charge.”

Rosa walked in the line of the Gospel: seeking the lost sheep, in a spirit of poverty.

“Every life devoted to money is a death. Rebirth lies in disinterestedness” (A. Camus).

In June 1867 cholera broke out in Piacenza. It lasted three months. In the province of Piacenza alone, 1,320 died.

The disease struck the elderly hardest.

So many girls and boys were left orphans.

The orphanages were overflowing. Families were sought to care for these orphans.

But many families took them only to profit from public money.

During the epidemic Rosa did not spare herself. She sent all her Sisters into the homes to nurse the stricken and took some orphan girls into the Mother House.

Then, with great courage and no less trust in Providence, she wrote to the mayor saying she was ready to take in — free of charge — all the orphan girls still without care.

“Providence is there...” Rosa thought. God never fails those who trust in him.

The mayor welcomed the offer enthusiastically and had a splendid reply sent to her, ringing with the city’s gratitude and Christian admiration.

Today we are struck by the prophetic gestures of bishops and cardinals who take orphans into their homes, hand over their palaces to become trade schools and let disaster victims sleep in their cathedrals.

A hundred years ago Rosa Gattorno’s gesture was no less prophetic: she did not hesitate to disturb the peace of the Mother House and the novitiate to throw the doors open to the orphan girls.

In the school of the Gospel the Servant of God had understood that Christianity means placing oneself on the axis of poverty.

Faith either moves mountains or transforms people

Within a few months the Mother House had taken in seventy girls. They lived on whatever help Providence sent from time to time. At this point the documents record a cluster of episodes that are hard to explain in human terms.

Is it perhaps the halo of legend that grows up around Rosa Gattorno, as around all great figures? We do not think so.

Probably it is the episodic fulfilment of Jesus’ words: “Truly, I say to you, if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there’, and it will move; and nothing will be impossible to you.”

We move no mountains, not even a hill, because we have no faith. Our unbelief paralyzes God’s very omnipotence.

“And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief” (Mt 13:58).

“... Jesus marvelled at him, and turning to the multitude that followed him, said, ‘I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith’” (Lk 7:9).

“Receive your sight; your faith has made you well” (Lk 18:42). “And when Jesus saw their faith he said to the paralytic...” (Mt 9:2).

“Daughter, your faith has made you well” (Mk 5:34). “If you can do anything, have pity on us and help us.” “If you can! All things are possible to him who believes.” Immediately the father of the child cried out: “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mk 9:22-24). “Go your way; your faith has made you well” (Mk 10:52). “And he said to the woman, ‘Your faith has saved you; go in peace’” (Lk 7:50).

One day, Sr A. Apollonia Marchetti relates, the coal for the kitchen ran out. The cook told Mother Gattorno, who answered: “Go — you will find enough.” The Sister went to the coal store, where shortly before there had been none at all, and found as much as was needed. Something similar happened with firewood: there was not a stick in the woodshed, and Sr Nazzarena, who had seen it empty and needed fuel, told the Servant of God. She replied: “You’re mistaken: there’s plenty. Come with me.” They went to the woodshed together and found it full.

The deaf hear and the dumb speak

Right after the cholera Rosa Gattorno had the chance to start another work: for deaf-mute girls.

Her deaf-mute daughter made her particularly sensitive to the problem.

Fr Eliseo Ghislandi, who had come to Piacenza for a few days for Carlotta’s First Communion, suggested she take in a deaf-mute girl from Milan named Villa, already taught by the Canossian Sisters, who could not safely go home because someone in her village was threatening her virtue.

“Signora Rosa,” Ghislandi said, “couldn’t this be the first stone of the building? Remember that you have a deaf-mute daughter. Villa would be an excellent companion for her, and if you want others just as good and honest, in time I can send you any number.”27

The Servant of God accepted enthusiastically. Villa came from Milan, a girl named Ravasi from Merate, and others from Parma and elsewhere.

They were all delighted with the care and affection they found in Rosa Gattorno and her Daughters. “I hear,” Fr Ghislandi wrote from Milan, “that Villa and Ravasi would like to come back to Milan to kiss my feet, they are so happy there. Tell them instead to kiss the crucifix for me.”

Rosa Gattorno trained specialized staff to give those girls a proper education.

She led them into intense prayer and established perpetual adoration of the Blessed Sacrament for them. Thus the “Laus perennis” began in the Mother House before Christ’s tabernacle, with those adoring daughters taking turns.

Some years later, when a special house was opened for them in Piacenza, Bishop Scalabrini, the great benefactor of the work, formed those unfortunate girls into a religious group with a habit of their own, as simple as that of the Daughters of Saint Anne. These adorers are bound by special ties to the Daughters of Saint Anne, living under their roof all their lives and repaying them a hundredfold, by unceasing prayer, for all they have received.

That family of deaf-mutes, now sadly extinct, was always very dear to the Servant of God, who kept it flourishing by always taking in new girls; even after her death it was regarded as the Institute’s most precious jewel in Piacenza.28

Let us take off our swaddling clothes

“If you want truly good, capable Sisters for the sick, ask Signora Rosa Gattorno to send you her Daughters.”

This advice had been given to the charity board running the hospital at Cento by a Capuchin Father who was its spiritual director.

The stupid, atheist century — as the nineteenth has been called — rejected the Church, yet with happy inconsistency asked for Sisters on the wards of suffering, beside their afflicted brothers.

The Cento hospital board’s request might well have raised doubts, since the congregation had been founded to protect girls at risk and visit the sick at home. After mature reflection and intense prayer Rosa Gattorno said “yes” to the call of the sick of Cento. She accepted and left at once with five postulants.

She had barely arrived when a letter full of encouragement came from Fr Firpo.

“This is the very place to which your crucified Love has long been drawing you by his grace.”

Nothing was ready at the Cento hospital. The first night Rosa had to sleep on the ward, in a bed from which a woman’s corpse had just been removed.

“In God’s works patience and sacrifice are needed,” she wrote to Piacenza.

No pay — only board, at first. Rosa stayed at Cento a month, happy. The sick were her world and her love. “I must tell you that I am very well and very happy in this dwelling so dear to me.”

In the evenings, after praying at length, she wrote letter after letter to her Daughters in Piacenza.

Correspondence would be one of her most meticulous concerns all her life. A letter makes us present to those we love who are far away; it carries them the beating of our heart.

The great educators all wrote many letters: St Jerome, St Francis de Sales, St John Bosco.

A letter can be a sheet anchor, a beat of the wing. In any case it is always a proof of love. If I did not love you I would not write to you. And the human heart is always hungry for love.

“It’s already past midnight,” she wrote to Bixio, “but I want to spend a little time with you, my dear. Steady patience, resignation: your mother is working for Jesus, so the daughter must feel the fatigue and the distance; but courage and peace! Call on Jesus...” And there follows a long series of detailed suggestions for peace of soul and religious observance.

To Rapallino she gave a lesson on detachment of heart that holds for all: “God,” she says, “likes sacrifices better than great promises... Jesus sacrificed himself for us and to the last evening drank the bitter cup: and we make such a fuss about being near rather than far! Come, my girls, let us take off our swaddling clothes...” So the little scattered flock felt the warm affection and vigorous encouragement of their one mother.

Late in March Rosa returned to Piacenza; but the heavy work of the Mother House, the crowd of novices, their training and other cares could not distract her from her concern for Cento. Hence the young Superior’s very frequent letters, in which one senses a mother’s anxiety over the dangers facing those inexperienced Daughters and reads the most detailed advice on religious conduct and lively reminders of the holiness of work done as service to Christ.

As for wine, let us agree not to drink too much

Rosa’s letters alternate notes of the loftiest spirituality with notes of tender humanity.

In those lines beat the heart of a woman of God and the tenderness of a mother.

“Blessed are you when the day comes when you can say: I am dying because I wore myself out in the works of Jesus... touching the poor with charity, for Jesus is found in those sick creatures... see that you are the servants of all...”

“Mind you eat enough...”

To understand Rosa Gattorno’s appeal one must reach this exquisite humanity of hers.

Young people instinctively flee the inhuman. They are drawn to those rich in humanity.

The saints draw crowds not only by their holiness but also by their humanity.

When St Augustine was asked whether it was a fault to take pleasure in the sense of smell, he replied: “As for perfumes, I do not worry much about them, except to welcome them in God’s name when they are present.”

“Although we read,” writes St Benedict in his Rule, “that wine is not a drink for monks, since monks cannot be persuaded of this, let us at least agree not to drink too much.”

“The great objection of our time against Christianity, the real source of the mistrust that seals off whole blocks of humanity from the Church’s influence, is not, strictly speaking, historical or theological difficulties; it is the suspicion that our religion makes its faithful inhuman.”

“They have confused the Church with a boarding school for well-bred young ladies”

The contemporary Russian writer Andrei Sinyavsky writes:

“Present-day Christianity sins by good manners. It cares only about not getting dirty, not seeming tactless; it fears mud, coarseness, frankness, preferring a meticulous mediocrity to everything else. What have we come to, drooling — the holy oil has turned into sickly treacle (the very word unction makes one queasy). We purse our lips piously and wait for the Lord to give us top marks for conduct.

“They have confused the Church of Christ with a boarding school for well-bred young ladies. In short, everything alive and brilliant has passed into the hands of vice; virtue is left to sigh and squeeze out a little tear. It has forgotten the fiery invectives of the Bible. But Christianity must be bold and call things by their name.

“The time has come to give up the little angels [?] of the aeroplanes. ‘Aeroplanes’ — not to ape the modern world but to surpass it.

“[…] so that they may become stronger and more […] angels

“Along this path one may fall into heresy. But today heresy is less dangerous than the root drying up.”

In this sense Rosa Gattorno did not sin by “good manners”...

When it was necessary to raise her voice, she knew how to raise it and make herself heard.

“Signor Rusconi, I need to speak with you...”

He was the manager of the Cento hospital...

“...For some time slanderous rumors have been circulating about my Sisters; letters are being checked, some made to disappear...”

The manager listened in astonishment. He had never heard the Servant of God speak in that tone.

“... Know, in the name of Jesus, that the charity I profess is honest... It has nothing to do with sinister ends... I ask you to show me the way to obtain redress for so great a slander.”

The vigorous protest had its effect, and the Sisters’ honor was vindicated by a public statement from the Vice-President of the charity board.

In 1868 the hospital’s management changed. Unacceptable conditions were put to the Daughters of Saint Anne, and at the end of 1868 the Servant of God chose to withdraw them.

The house at Cento closed, but the one at Sampierdarena opened.

Called by Fr Angelo Ricchini, Rosa arrived there on the evening of 12 November 1868. Work began at once: nursing the sick and caring for poor and abandoned young people.2930

In the spring of 1869 the Sampierdarena community moved to the nearby Villa Gattorno, rented to them by the Servant of God’s father. There were many girls: thirty boarders and many more day pupils. Several conversions of adults, some at the point of death, show how devotedly Rosa’s Daughters worked.

While she was busy founding and organizing the Sampierdarena house, a heavy blow fell on Rosa Gattorno.

One of the first five companions — the one in whom she placed the greatest trust, so much that she had made her Superior of the Piacenza house — began to wage open war on the foundress, spreading slanders far and wide against the foundation and against Rosa Gattorno personally: she was the cause of all the Institute’s misfortunes, she was starving the Daughters, she was, in short, the Institute’s real ruin.

The letter with all this venom reached Sampierdarena on the very day the new house was opened.

Rosa suffered terribly but did not think of retaliating. Instead she wrote with great humility:

“My dear! If you knew what pain it is for me... to think that I am your ruin, your scandal, that I serve only to spoil the Lord’s work: I feel my heart torn apart, and I keep thanking my God for having taken me out and sent me far from you. So you will receive more generous Providence from Heaven, without this most infamous woman holding it back. And yet, my dear, I can assure you that in all this wretch has done and said, her thought was always for your good.

“Forgive me all I have done to you and obtain the same forgiveness for me from the community...”

The story of a hundred francs

“Dear Mother, I am writing to report on my usual business. This morning I left the house at eight and went round until eleven without getting anything. I, a poor Daughter of Saint Anne, short of patience, had almost decided to go home empty-handed... I walked a stretch thinking about this... Then I thought: let’s try going to Marchioness Cattaneo’s. She gave us a hundred francs.”

The writer is Sr Serafina, the Sister charged with collecting alms in Genoa.

Rosa Gattorno particularly wanted a house in Genoa, her native city.

In the spring of 1871 she finally succeeded: a small, poor house of nurses caring for the sick in their homes free of charge.

Hard times, heroic times. Three small rented rooms. The only resource: begging.

The founding of a religious house is never an official function either, with bows, brass bands and attendance fees: its path is no stroll, whether archaeological or touristic.

Another testimony to the poverty of the Genoa house.

“There were days,” a Sister recalled many years later, “when even bread was lacking; even so we were all cheerful and worked hard. We sat on the floor for want of chairs; and I remember, as if it were now, how happy we were together with that woman, in whom something heavenly shone through.”

Poverty and joy: an echo of the Little Flowers of St Francis. Whoever cannot laugh is a slave, even if he rules.

The year 1871 saw another foundation: Ferrara. It was opened on 10 October by Cardinal Vannicelli himself, Archbishop of that city.

Ferrara soon became a large family. In a letter to Fr Agostino Donadio, Mother Rosa speaks of a hundred and eighty-nine girls being brought up in the fear of God, a passion for the Church and love for the Pope. Those girls have hope. They are the future of civil society and of the Church community.

Then came Nizza Monferrato: a hospital and schools.

The balance after the first six months of life: six houses scattered across Italy.

Progress was rapid.

Now, however, a halt was needed.

The congregation needed precise Rules. But before the Rules there is another story — a story of attempts on her life.

It reads like a novel. In fact it is a drama of malice on one side and forgiveness on the other.

Rosmini once asked a young man, who would later become President of the Senate, whether he loved the truth.

“Yes,” the young man replied, “I love the truth, or at least I want to love it.”

“Good,” Rosmini concluded. “Then prepare to suffer a great deal.”

Rosa Gattorno was prepared to suffer for truth and for love. But she did not imagine the cup of suffering would be so bitter.

At the end of her life she would tell her daughters: “Do not let trials, slanders, worries or anguish make you fail in your holy vocation... I too was slandered, despised, ill-treated, and not the slightest thought against my holy vocation ever entered my mind.”

“Slandered, despised, ill-treated”: there is the summary of her whole Calvary. The college of the Apostles had its Judas. The Daughters of Saint Anne too had their Judas at their birth.

This was the Sister who had written the Mother a letter full of insults and slander while she was at Sampierdarena.

Her heart grew ever more poisoned, until she hatched a real conspiracy.

A trial that was a complete farce

March 1869. Rosa was at Sampierdarena. Among her other sorrows was that of her son Alessandro, now sixteen and seriously ill: there was talk of amputating a leg.

A letter arrived from Piacenza summoning her at once to the Mother House.

She left that very evening and, contrary to custom, quite alone. She reached Piacenza station at half past eleven and at midnight was knocking at the door of the Mother House. They kept her waiting and made difficulties about letting her in. Once inside she asked for the Superior, surprised not to see her, and was told she was in bed. Not having the key to her own little room, she went up to the Superior and asked first of all what was wrong — was she ill? The answer was a curt no. The other Sisters with her stood there silent, with an air of mystery and embarrassment.

“But what is it? Why are you all so upset?” the Mother asked.

No one answered; only the cook, who had followed close behind her since she came in, pressed near her, whispering: “Mother! Poor Mother!”

But no one hurried to break the ice. No one thought of offering anything or inviting the Mother to rest. The night was bitterly cold, and Rosa, chilled to the bone, asked for a room to retire to. She was told to go to the guest quarters.

Rosa Gattorno then withdrew to the chapel and stayed there all night.

Morning came at last. She received Communion and, after her spiritual exercises, went to the Superior.

“What is it?” she asked. “Speak.”

“I don’t know,” she replied.

“What? And where is Father Tornatore? Call me when he comes.” The Superior shook her head and murmured: “He isn’t coming; he won’t come any more.”

“What?... But what on earth is going on?”

At last Fr Tornatore, sent for several times, sent word that he would come towards evening, but not to stay.313233

He came, went into the parlor, called Mother Gattorno and at once forbade her Holy Communion. He mentioned some very grave accusations the Superior had made against her, and left.

“I wept a little,” the Mother says at this point. “Then, reflecting on what those accusations were about, I grew calm. But thinking that for fourteen and a half years I had never missed Holy Communion, I felt great sorrow. I obeyed. In the evening, in my dear poor room, I scourged this monster of a body.”

The next morning at nine Fr Tornatore came to hold a kind of trial, in the place where the Sisters usually made their confessions: two small rooms connected by a little grille. On one side sat Tornatore, with the Servant of God before him; on the other, in turn, those who had made the accusations. The Father read aloud a very long report that took five whole hours, from nine to noon and from one to three. Mother Rosa listened on her knees.

In the afternoon, while the accusations against the Mother were still being read, the Sister cook suddenly burst into the room. She broke down in tears and protested: “The Mother is innocent... it’s all a conspiracy...”

On the other side of the grille another Sister threw herself on her knees and, weeping, begged forgiveness: “The Mother is innocent... It was the Superior who forced me to sign...”

Fr Tornatore, as if waking from a dream, realized he had been the victim of a trap.

The Mother embraced her repentant Daughters, then withdrew to her room to pray.

For three hours, clasping her crucifix, she wept and prayed, shaken from head to foot by a terrible convulsion that racked her whole body.

She had been fasting for twenty-four hours. She would fast twelve hours more so as to receive Communion the next morning.

No punishment for the Superior.

She sent her to run another house. Only two years later was she dismissed from the Institute, after other grave failings had shown that she was utterly unsuited to religious life.

We do not know her name. It appears in no register of the Institute, and probably Mother Gattorno herself destroyed every trace of the affair, even in the writings of other Sisters.

Are you ready to be crucified?

The Franco-Israeli Association once asked Fr Gauthier, founder of the Carpenter Brothers of Nazareth, to give a lecture in Haifa to an audience of three or four hundred Jews of every social class and every persuasion.

Fr Gauthier spoke on “Israel, meeting-point of East and West”. The chairman, Gurevic, had cordially introduced him as a Catholic priest and told the audience in Hebrew not to be surprised if his words were those of a Christian.

The Father spoke with great frankness. He quoted the answer the sculptor Nathan had given him to the question “What is a Jew?”: “Someone who carries the Cross, but without Christ.”

He also quoted Archbishop Fulton Sheen’s words on New York radio: “The East has taken the Cross without Christ, and the West has taken Jesus without the Cross.”

The audience followed the lecture closely.

Then came a crossfire of questions, among them: “Are you ready to be crucified?”

The questioner was an old workman who had suffered much in life; he had carried the Cross without Christ.

Two more crosses awaited Rosa: poison and the dagger.

In the mornings Rosa took only a cup of coffee. Once, from certain signs, she suspected the cup contained poison. She drank it all the same, but at once was seized by agonizing pains. The doctor came and saved her.

“I must report this to the civil authorities,” the doctor said.

“I beg you,” the Mother pleaded, “don’t speak of it to anyone.”

The poisoner’s name has not been recorded.

In the Piacenza house there was a Sister from Foligno.

One evening, while the Servant of God was praying in her room, this Sister came in with a knife hidden under her habit.

Rosa looked her in the eye and said: “Stop. Do not do what you have in mind. Put down at once what you have in your hand. Remember you have a soul to save.”

The wretched woman, struck by words that revealed what she believed was utterly secret, knelt down, drew from under her habit the hand holding the knife, laid down the weapon and wept.

“Now go down to the chapel and ask God’s forgiveness. We’ll see each other tomorrow.”

The next day she herself took the Sister to Cortemaggiore to make a retreat with other Sisters of that community.

When the retreat was over she called her again and said: “I can see you are not suited to our Institute. Now you are in God’s grace: go back to your family.”

That knife is still kept in Piacenza.

Writing the truth with the blood of our veins

“If truth,” writes Papini in his Life of Christ, “is to remain on earth for ever, so that no one can ever forget it, you must write it in blood; and because truths come from blood, only with the blood of our veins can truths be written on the pages of the earth, so that the footsteps of men and the rains of the centuries do not fade them.”

Rosa Gattorno went on writing in blood. More sufferings.

“There were fireworks on every side,” she says, “and I was without comfort, alone.”

A dispute broke out with the priests Richini of Genoa. It would end in court.

The Archbishop of Genoa, Mgr Salvatore Magnasco, intervened. Rosa won the case, and the Archbishop gave her a letter declaring that the Servant of God was in the right.

Illnesses struck several Sisters.

Creditors suddenly appeared demanding immediate payment.

And Rosa redoubled her penances and prayers.

Only that dignity is real which is not diminished by the indifference of others

Hammarskjöld, the first Secretary-General of the UN, who died tragically in the Congo while hurrying to bring peace among the rebels, writes in his diary Markings:

“Never arrived: a higher mission is only a higher class in this school, where you draw near to an examination of which no one will ever know anything, because you will be entirely alone in it.

“Your position never gives you the right to command. Only the duty to live so that others can receive your command without being humiliated.

“Only that dignity is real which is not diminished by the indifference of others.”

Rosa Gattorno lived these principles deeply.

She lowered herself before the Sisters who harmed her and forgave them, just as she humbled herself before Sisters she feared she had offended and asked their pardon.

At Sampierdarena, at a meeting in Fr Tornatore’s presence, she upheld an opinion contrary to that of her other Daughters present.

She feared she had failed in charity. So the next morning, “before receiving her God, she called the Superior and her assistant to her room one after the other and asked their forgiveness for having opposed them”.

The needs of her foundation grew daily as houses and vocations multiplied.

Correspondingly Rosa increased her penances.

We have already mentioned them; here are some more.

She wanted to be ever more conformed, outwardly too, to Christ Crucified. So she even tried hanging herself on a large cross.

She spent the last days of Holy Week shut in her little room, immersed in prayer, fasting and penance, inflicting on herself as many as 1,600 strokes of the discipline.

She bound herself by vow not to eat fruit — first a temporary vow, then a perpetual one.

And yet her health was far from robust. Migraines and fainting fits, fevers and irregular pulse tormented her almost constantly.

But for her, as for every person of God, St Paul’s principle held: “When I am weak, then I am strong.”

Don Primo Mazzolari, who may be compared with Rosa Gattorno for a life woven through with trials and misunderstandings, left us a precious rule for checking whether we are on the right path — a rule that, one might say, sums up and explains Rosa Gattorno’s whole life:

“When you gain nothing but suffering, when you alone pay the price, the road is the right one.”

Rules are to a congregation what style is to a writer.

But there are writers and writers.

And Manzoni is not Papini.

There are Sisters and Sisters.

The Rules are the mark that distinguishes them, because they set the goals to be reached and the pace to be kept.

The Rules of the Daughters of Saint Anne were not written by the foundress.

The Pope had told her he wanted them soon. She set to work with a will, but got nowhere.

“I prayed a great deal, but I felt nothing.”

So she decided to entrust the drafting to Fr Tornatore. He accepted with a smile, set to work and finished in a few months.

At the beginning of February 1868 the foundress took a copy to the Bishop of Piacenza, Mgr Ranza, and on the 24th of that month sent a second copy to Rome. The Bishop approved the Rules at once; Cardinal Consolini merely acknowledged receipt of the manuscript.

Mother Gattorno, strengthened by the Bishop’s approval, had the Rules printed and sent them to the bishops and all the houses.

For three years all went smoothly, and the Servant of God received no objections. Fr Tornatore had by now become the spiritual director of the Daughters of Saint Anne, guiding and helping them in every kind of task.

When there was a danger that his superiors would transfer him because his teaching term at the College of S. Lazzaro in Piacenza had ended, Rosa Gattorno rushed to the Bishop.

“Your Excellency, couldn’t you put in a word?...”

“To what effect?”

“To point out that the Father is like the Director of the Institute — indeed one might say its Founder... And so to obtain that he not be moved from Piacenza, and even that he be able to devote himself entirely to the Daughters of Saint Anne.”

So little did Rosa care for the honor of being called foundress! Fr Tornatore, on the other hand, called her so: in a letter of 1880 he urged the novice mistress to instil in the young Sisters “love, reverence and devotion for the center of the Institute, the Mother General, who is also the Foundress”.

Fr Tornatore stayed in Piacenza for the time being, and late in 1870 Mother Rosa wanted to present the Rules to the Holy See for approval. She asked Cardinal Consolini for permission to go to Rome, but he advised her to wait because of the painful events that had befallen the Papal States.

A terrible disappointment

The journey to Rome was put off until the following year.3435

She was received in audience by Pope Pius IX on 4 June 1871.

She presented the Rules to him, and “he told me he would read them, encouraging me all the while”, she writes in her Memoirs.

She returned to Piacenza full of confidence. But the days passed and no approval came from Rome.

“I commend to you,” she wrote to Mgr Wanstienkist on 15 July 1871, “the well-known matter of the Rules; I am anxiously awaiting a line that will console me.”

Consolation indeed! A terrible disappointment was on its way.

The consultors’ examination and vote went against approval. But worse followed: on 28 December a letter from Fr Manfredini to Fr Tornatore brought this news:

“The Rules presented to the Sacred Congregation have been passed by it to the Holy Office.”

The greater one is, the better one knows how to obey

Mother Gattorno hurried to Rome with her secretary, Sr Vincenza Rapallino.

She went to the Sacred Congregation for news but was met with banter. Indeed one of the officials, alluding to the dialogue form in which the Rules were presented, asked her almost mockingly: “Do you always talk to Saint Anne?”

“What shame I suffered,” the Mother writes, “together with my secretary! I no longer had the courage to show myself anywhere.”

She returned to Piacenza in anguish. She had barely got back when a new, inhuman trial broke upon her.

On the evening of 19 February 1872 Mother Gattorno received from Mgr Mariano Wanstienkist, secretary to Cardinal Vannicelli, Protector of the Daughters of Saint Anne, a letter that stunned her like a thunderbolt. She was secretly ordered to withdraw all copies of the Rules distributed to bishops and Sisters and burn them, together with all the copies in the house. She was further ordered to remove from the Institute the author of the Rules, who was to be “removed and kept away from any interference in or direction of the Institute”.

For a leader, being asked to disown one’s own acts is martyrdom.

Rosa felt torn apart. And Fr Tornatore, to whom she conveyed Rome’s order that same evening, felt as devastated as she did. The obedience of faith sometimes costs heroism. All the copies of the Rules were burned. It was Abraham’s sacrifice! As she performed this extreme act of fidelity, the foundress said, dreamily yet firmly: “These rules will come out of the flames.”

And they did come out — today, at the gentle breath of the Spirit, who has led the Daughters of Saint Anne back to the sources of their spirituality in the setting of Vatican II. Discovered in a copy that providentially escaped the flames and studied in the light of the “return to the sources” called for by the Second Vatican Council, that Rule — though lacking the necessary juridical element and written in a style unusual for its literary genre — in fact contains the true, specific charism of the Institute. Its content is set out with a wealth of spiritual motives and biblical insights, albeit in the author’s own idiom, and today the Daughters of Saint Anne recognize in that synthesis the spirituality of the “Poor of Yahweh”. But Fr Tornatore was not understood. And he had enemies. Two events brought about the decline of his reputation, with accusations and vile slanders. Both Bishop Scalabrini and Pope Pius IX defended him against that shameful campaign — a great comfort at least in the last years of the Father, marked by the cross, who died a holy death on 31 January 1895.

“You’ve had a good thrashing”

36

The next morning she wrote to Cardinal Vannicelli’s secretary, informing him that she had carried out the orders and asking permission to go to Rome.

“May God’s will be done on our heads; and I, a wretched creature, with my head to the ground, adore all his dispositions and submit to the will of the Church.”

This time she found Rome better disposed. Her obedience had shown everyone the spirit of the Servant of God.

The new secretary of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, Mgr Vitelleschi, received her kindly.

“You’ve had a good thrashing...”

“... but everything can be put right. The Pope wants the Institute to live and spread...”

The Pope too received her with great fatherliness.

“Pius IX’s words,” the Mother would say, “gave me life.”

Cardinal Vannicelli, Protector of the Daughters of Saint Anne, was Archbishop of Ferrara. Rosa arranged with him that she would go to Ferrara and there, under the guidance of his Vicar, Mgr Giordani, work on drafting the Rules.

“Mother, wouldn’t it be good, before we start writing, to go round all the houses of your Institute and see their needs and requirements, so as to make the Rules as concrete as possible?”

A long, laborious visitation, but consoled by the good spirit in the various communities.

Painful, on the other hand, was the cold reception she received from the Archbishop of Genoa, probably suspicious and ill-disposed because of the business of the Rules.

He received her on 23 March. He did not even ask her to sit down. A few words, distant and curt. He would not even give her permission to have the community chapel blessed.

“Patience,” the Mother writes. “At once I made an offering to my Eternal Father and, full of resignation and peace, I clung to Jesus.”

Back in Ferrara she set to writing the Rules and dashed them off in seven days.

Too quickly. The result was a piece of work that would once again be rejected.

In this world there are those who make history and those who write it.

There are those who live love and those who write about love.

Rosa Gattorno lived love, but she was not made to give others the Rules of Love.

Each has his own charism.

Besides, this was nothing new in the history of congregations. In the same period other foundresses could not manage to draw up the Rules of their congregations.

On 18 June the manuscript reached Rome.

After six months, in December 1872, Rome’s answer came: everything had to be redone.37

With the refusal came a piece of advice: to give the task to Fr Fava, a Jesuit well known and highly esteemed for his learning and piety, but old and extremely busy.

Months went by and Fr Fava did nothing. Not that he was unwilling — he had no time.

“Monsignor, would you be willing to take it on?”

Mgr Vitelleschi felt great pity for this Sister who had been struggling for years over those blessed Rules.

He took the matter to heart and saw it through, entrusting the drafting of the Rules to Fr Raimondo Bianchi, Procurator General of the Dominicans. And on 12 June 1874 the Constitutions were at last approved ad experimentum by Cardinal Vannicelli.

Two years later the Institute received the “Decree of Praise” from the Holy See.

The Mother gathered the community and gave them the great news.

Her heart was flooded with joy and gratitude to God. Only she knew what those Rules had cost her.

Then again, ideas are worth not what they yield but what they cost.

In her Memoirs she would write:

“The irons I keep under my knees when I pray; the meatless food I take, and so poorly; the irons I wear on my arms and legs and the sores they have made — all this I offer you, that you may grant that your Institute never fail in the observance of the holy Rules until the end of the world.”38

While Mother Gattorno was busy with drafting the Constitutions and securing their approval, the Institute’s expansion came to a halt.

Fewer postulants were accepted for several months. No new houses were opened. 1872 was a year of recollection and of deepening the spirituality proper to the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Rosa’s difficulties and uncertainties had some basis: the typical defects of every foundation at its birth.

Growing pains.

Every living organism goes through them. But the Mother, in her deep humility, blamed herself for the crisis:

“The cause of your trouble is me, for having given in too much to your wishes.”

We have some notes of the spiritual conferences Mother Gattorno gave her Daughters in 1872.

“The Daughter of Saint Anne must be, as our Holy Father Pius IX told me, an apostle who preaches the faith by her good deeds and good example — to the devout, to further their fervor more and more; to those who are not devout, to draw them to devotion or at least make them Christians.”

For Mother Gattorno the religious is above all a witness who acts by her life rather than by words.

Rosa Gattorno had realized that the people of her time hungered for love more than for apologetics. They did not want arguments to grasp but wounds to touch.

Like the Apostle Thomas.

“Unless I put my hand into his wounds, I will not believe.”

The First Vatican Council had already declared that the Church, “by her eminent holiness, her inexhaustible fruitfulness in every good, her catholic unity..., is of herself a great and perpetual motive of credibility and an irrefutable witness of her divine mission.” For believers and unbelievers alike she is a “sign” among the nations.

But the Second Vatican Council prefers the expressions “witness of life” and “living witness”, and speaks of “living witnesses” of Christ. The term “witness” is, with a few others (people of God, service, unity in charity, signs of the times, paschal mystery, etc.), one of the Council’s favorite terms. Its use of the category of “witness” to denote holiness of life is not merely accidental, for it is habitual. It clearly shows the Council’s wish to respond to the sensibility and mentality of modern man. Modern man is repelled by a holiness conceived as the Platonic reproduction of an abstract ideal. For him holiness is essentially movement and life.39

The Council does not merely invite Christians to the witness of a holy life; it explains what that witness consists in. “Called by God” and led “by the spirit of the Gospel”, Christians, it says, are invited to “make Christ known to others, especially by the testimony of a life resplendent in faith, hope and charity”.

“The sight of such a life, where word and deed correspond so perfectly, arouses in the onlooker the desire to come into contact with the universe of values he has discovered. The encounter with Christ in his living witness reaches into the other’s deepest self and invites him to repeat the experience of salvation in Jesus Christ.”

In one of the boldest books of biblical exegesis, Pierre Benoit writes:

“The people we speak to can tell very well whether we are reciting a doctrine learned by heart, the way a pedlar tries to sell his wares without believing in them himself. If we are only propagandists, no one will believe us. But if they sense that we live what we say, that we have met the object of our faith, that our whole life is consecrated to that Father, that Son, that Spirit, then we shall be effective witnesses and we shall be believed.”

And this is essentially a splendid paraphrase of what Bernanos said far more bluntly: “A writer is either a witness or a nuisance.”4041

The Christian too is either a witness or a nuisance.

“Fire! Fire! Sisters, they’re burning you!”

On 11 August 1872 Mgr Mariano Wanstienkist wrote to the Mother: “Mgr Vitelleschi (secretary of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars) sees no difficulty in your opening other houses...”

The Servant of God set to work at once. So at the beginning of 1873, in barely three months, the Institute accepted six new foundations: a hospital at Ovada, a school at Foligno, and three schools and a house for domestic servants in Rome.

They had only just arrived at Foligno. One night they heard shouting: “Fire! Fire! Sisters, fire! They’re burning you!”

The Sisters jumped up and rushed to the door of the burning house.

The Freemasons, very numerous in the town, had smeared the door with petroleum and set it alight. The Sisters put out the flames with water and sand.

The next morning the carabinieri came to inspect and found a note posted up: “Shut down this brothel of nuns protected by the Duke of Sora Piombino and Cavaliere Morotti. Goodbye for now.”

In the spring of 1873 three houses were opened in Rome. Here too, dire poverty.

“We,” a Superior wrote from Rome, “are as if in the middle of the sea: wind and water come in from every side and we are always walking through water.”

By the end of 1873, after barely seven years of existence, the Daughters of Saint Anne numbered more than 200. Foundations multiplied: 5 in 1874, as many in 1875, 9 in 1876, 13 in 1877, and so on at an average of 10 houses a year.

Their field of action was now wide: central Italy, Piedmont, Liguria, Lombardy, the Veneto, Sicily.

Before Rosa Gattorno’s death Sicily alone would have 60 houses of the Institute, 10 of them in Palermo.

Passing through Rome on her way to Naples to start a new foundation, the Servant of God was received in audience by Pius IX, together with the eight Sisters accompanying her.

“Here are the Daughters of Saint Anne, my ragamuffins,” the Pope exclaimed with a smile. He chatted with them kindly and gave them some advice.

“Be apostles and be watchful, for the devil does not sleep. Call often on St Michael the Archangel; he will defend and help you, and with his help you will do great good.”

When the Servant of God died in 1900 she had founded 318 houses in Italy, 43 in America and 7 in Africa — 368 houses in all, with 4,000 Daughters of Saint Anne.

The witnesses who guide history

What was the secret of this rapid expansion?

It is not easy to answer. There was, undoubtedly, God’s blessing: that is the first and surest secret. But certain historical, sociological and psychological factors also played a part.42

In Rosa Gattorno’s day health care as provided by the State today did not exist. So anything that met the needs of the sick was welcomed and encouraged, especially where anticlericalism was less rampant.

The same must be said of the care and education of the young.

Real education was in the hands of religious.

But one must also take into account a psychological, human factor: the personality of the foundress.

There are people who do not need to speak; it is enough that they exist. Their presence is already a call, so great is the radiance they give off and the attraction they exert. They are the witnesses who guide history.

At the origin of all the great institutions of the Church there is almost always one of these witnesses.

Rosa Gattorno had a whole cluster of virtues bound to strike everyone she met.

First of all, consistency. She lived what she said. When she spoke, her life echoed.

She certainly did not deserve Jesus’ biting invective against those who say and do not do. She practiced what she preached. Her Daughters would comment: “Throughout her long government she ruled the Institute well not only by word, instruction and decision, but above all by her example. They called her the living Rule.”

Nothing is achieved by orders alone

Another side of her personality was an exquisite humanity — a very modern side of Rosa Gattorno. She anticipated the insights of modern “personalism”.43

One of modern man’s achievements is “personalism”.

Today the word “personalism”, with its adjective “personalist”, is given a much broader sense than is commonly understood. In the new sense “personalism” means a tendency to present the human person in his concreteness, richness and dignity as the basis of social ethics.

Personalism makes two demands on the Christian: first, a greater understanding and appreciation of the human person as Christianity understands him; second, greater sensitivity to the historical, environmental and biological circumstances in which that person lives.

Today anyone who wants to influence people must know the situation of those he addresses in order to present the Christian ideal better; for that ideal, though above “history”, must also enter into it.

St Thomas protested with his robust common sense against those who forget they have a body.

“Man is neither angel nor beast, and whoever tries to play the angel plays the beast” (Pascal).

Here is how St Francis de Sales writes to St Jane de Chantal: “I truly believe there is no warmer or more tender soul in the world — to put it plainly, no more loving soul — than mine; for so God has been pleased to form my heart.”

Precisely because they are fully human, the saints are never pedantic, petty or harsh.

“It is better to err on the side of leniency than of severity,” said St Francis de Sales.

“Father,” a little boy asked St John Vianney, “must I study my lesson or can I go and play?”

“Play, my child; it is the right of your age.”

St Augustine writes: “Paulus et pater et mater est” — “In the Apostle Paul beat together a father’s heart and a mother’s heart.”

Humanity, understanding, accommodation and patience were the criteria by which Mother Rosa judged whether a Sister was fit to be a Superior.

In an instruction to Superiors she wrote:

“To bear patiently with your sisters’ characters, to take on their sorrows and labors, to try to relieve them with acts of kindness, without weakness or grimaces but with true charity and a mother’s love: this is your mission.”

And again:

“The Superiors of the houses must be so many little mothers to the Sisters, so that, having left their mothers and families, the religious find in the Superior a motherly affection that wins their trust; and so, receiving comfort in their sorrows, they will not feel the need to pour out their hearts to others.”

Sometimes her rebukes were strong — but only when the good spirit of the Institute was at stake.

And even then she tried to save the Sisters’ face. Never animosity or anger. Never public rebukes.4445

A Superior had had to rebuke her community publicly for a serious fault, but she had gone too far. When the Servant of God heard of it she wrote at once: “Oh, for pity’s sake, treat your daughters with more of a mother’s love, without embittering them. Take them calmly and tell them to be good: remember they are poor creatures working for Saint Anne. My daughter, honors have done your heart harm: see, see whether it isn’t true that they are the plague of our souls.”

To another Superior, who fretted too much over how her house was going, she gave this wise advice: “You always write to me sad and full of resentment: I tell you all your anxieties are based on falsehood... I recommend gentleness to you, for that is the true character of a daughter of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate. If we are to imitate the Mother, that is what we must do... Courage, patience, resignation to God’s will: so we shall give good example. Superiors are the shadow of the other religious: they all run after it and go the way the shadow shows them. Do you see a quick-tempered mother who is always shouting and always wears a sad face? All the children do the same, and order no longer reigns in that family. Patience, docility and resignation are the qualities God wants in a Superior. If you are upset, run to church and cry out with Jesus; weep; and then, when you have dried your tears, back to work again, all things to all, full of sweetness so as to produce it in others.”4647

Anyone reading the minutes of the Municipality of La Paz in Bolivia comes across this resolution:

“Profit cannot produce all the self-denial needed to care for and help humanity in its terrible sufferings. Only Christian charity is capable of this great sacrifice, with the hope of an immortal reward, the desire for a prize higher than any earthly one. Until the unfortunate patients in these houses are watched over and nursed by the Sisters of Charity, these missionaries of Providence whom some have called angels on earth, the service will never improve as much as we wish. The Municipality must therefore make every effort to bring these holy women to the country.”

This document ought to be forwarded to certain anticlerical bigwigs on certain boards of our hospitals.

They see only the Sisters’ faults and limitations. They ought to do without them for a year. They would soon launch an appeal like that of the Municipality of La Paz.48

Bolivia calls Italy. Bolivia is looking for Sisters.

The search was entrusted to a Franciscan, Fr Virginio Rocchi, who arrived with a pocketful of authorizations from the Bolivian bishops and government.

But his was no easy task. France... nothing. Spain... nothing. In Rome they told him: go to Piacenza. For two years Mother Gattorno had been preparing suitable Sisters. When Fr Rocchi arrived she agreed at once. The agreement was signed by both parties on 19 October 1878 — a historic date, the first page of the missionary history of the Daughters of Saint Anne.
