On the morning of 23 November 1878 the first sixteen Daughters of Saint Anne sailed for Bolivia on the steamer Esperia, led by their Superior, Sr A. Giuseppa Troni.

A very long sea voyage. They landed at the port of Mollendo in Peru on 17 June 1879.

From there, partly by rail and partly across Lake Titicaca, they reached La Paz on the 20th of that month.

A great, festive welcome from everyone: government, clergy and people.

“Las abnegadas madrecitas de la caridad have arrived...”

Speeches, articles, receptions.

The hosanna. Then would come the crucifige of the “terrible everyday”, of hardships and misunderstandings.

As in every human life and venture. The La Paz hospital: what a torment! There were not even rooms for the Sisters. The journey, hardship, the climate: after barely two weeks two Sisters fell ill and died. Imagine the Mother’s grief.

To replace them she at once prepared other missionary Sisters to leave the following year, choosing as Superior Sr A. Camilla Valentini, who ran the hospital at Borgo S. Donnino (now Fidenza).

The account Sr A. Camilla herself — later the fourth Superior General of the Institute — gives of being summoned to Piacenza by Mother Rosa is so lively and frank that it is worth quoting in full:

“In March 1882 I was at Borgo S. Donnino (Parma) when my Most Reverend Mother asked whether I was willing to go to America.

“‘No, no,’ I replied firmly, ‘unless America comes here.’

“At that time many Sisters had asked to go to the foreign missions, but none of them could serve as Superior, and no Superior in the houses was willing to leave Europe; so the Mother thought of me and sent for me.

“I was afraid she would repeat the request just mentioned; out of sheer duty I prepared to leave (for Piacenza), paying no attention even to a rather serious ailment that had kept me in bed for a fortnight.

“In fact, after a fall, a bone in my left leg had been fractured, and the leg had quickly become swollen and black, so that the doctors spoke of incipient gangrene and thought an operation necessary.

“But, as I said, when the Mother’s summons came I did not stop to think: staggering, with others holding me up, I dragged myself to the railway station, which was very close (to the hospital), and, as God willed, an hour later the first obedience was done.49

“I cannot describe the pain I suffered on that journey; but remembering the tenderness the good Mother had for all of us, I hoped to be treated or examined by other doctors or by her herself.

“Not at all; nobody asked about my ailment, which was very serious.

“I was shown into the Mother’s little workroom, but she did not see me at once. She said: ‘Stay here; I’m going to pray; then I’ll come back to you.’

“And off she went, quite calmly, to the church, and stayed there more than an hour.

“Meanwhile there were people with me who talked to me — indirectly, yes, but pointedly — about America.

“And what did the Mother have to ask the Lord in such long prayers, while I suffered with my foot and my heart in turmoil?

“I learned later, remembering one of her favorite sayings: ‘Do you want graces from God? Do you want answers from him? Pray, pray and do penance.’

“In that hour so rich in blessings for the Institute and in loving exchange between Jesus and our Mother, I sat there groaning inwardly with suppressed pain and was almost on the point of giving way to impatience.

“But here came the dear Mother, and as if continuing a conversation just interrupted: ‘Did you hear, my daughter, all the lovely things about America?’

“‘Yes, Mother,’ I replied, ‘and I’m glad for the Institute, for the honor of opening a new house.’

“‘And would you like to go?’

“‘No, Mother, really! And besides, how could I, with my foot in such a state?’ Inwardly I was trembling at the enormous responsibility about to crush me.

“I, still so young (I was twenty-seven), at the head of a community of no small importance, and in distant lands!

“I clung to my physical infirmity almost as to a sheet anchor, hoping to be excused from so heavy a burden.

“‘... So, my daughter, will you go?’...

“‘Mother,’ I at once replied firmly, ‘it’s impossible! I’m ill; I haven’t been able to stand for a long time.’

“‘Don’t think about your ailment; God will see to that. Won’t you do me this favor, then?’

“‘Mother, if it’s to do you a favor, here I am! Do with me as you wish.’

“‘Good girl,’ she replied at once, stroking my cheek. ‘The Lord bless you. Believe me, you are doing me a kindness, for I have no one else if you don’t accept.’

“After receiving several official and affectionate instructions from her, I returned to Borgo S. Donnino to teach the Superior who was to replace me the bookkeeping, the running of the house and everything else necessary.

“But because of the strain of too much moving about and the agitation of my heart, the surgeon, seeing me back in a far from reassuring state, was not only alarmed but flew into such a rage that he burst out: ‘Go on, do as many stupid things as you like on your own account, and if you want to die, then die!’

“It should be noted that from the time I was with my Mother the ailment stayed the same, but it was serious and I suffered a great deal.

“It was my duty to hand over my office, and I did so quickly, limping between an armchair and a pallet.

“Here I was at the Mother House, worse than ever, and I stayed so for about a month and a half without the slightest treatment.

“Then, seeing that preparations for departure were really being made, I said one day: ‘But Mother, you don’t know what state I’m in, because you’ve never looked at me!’

“‘Do God’s will; he will see to healing you! It’s nothing. I repeat, don’t think about anything; he wants you in America.’

“They were sublime words, but they stayed words and did nothing for my terrible pain; until one day she called me and said: ‘I promised your parents to have your portrait made. Go out with Sr A. Angelica to the photographer.’

“‘How can I?’ I replied, between astonishment and pain.

“Those present saw that my leg and foot were so swollen they had lost their natural shape. It was impossible to put a shoe on or bind them in any way.

“‘Go, I tell you; obedience works miracles. You, Sr A. Angelica, bring her shoes; and you, put them on!’

“‘Mother, won’t you believe me? Look now.’

“‘Obey.’

“I bowed my head to the great word and took the shoes, and while my kind Sister bent down to help me, I — as if in a dream — could not understand what was about to happen to me.

“Gently the leg and foot, so swollen and black a moment before, grew slender, and without my noticing, my foot slipped smoothly into the shoe that a few minutes earlier had seemed much too small.

“Astonishment, joy and trembling seized me, and I looked at the Mother, who, calm as ever, exclaimed: ‘You see? It’s true that obedience works miracles! I told you the Lord would heal you. But not a word, mind! Your gratitude is owed to him alone.’

“And so, suddenly healed, I went out and walked long distances without feeling any pain.

“Nor did I ever afterwards feel anything at all to suggest how serious my ailment had been.”

In the days after the healing the Mother gave the new Superior her instructions for the work entrusted to her:

“As for the language, do as best you can; I have no Sisters who know Spanish; you’ll learn it in time.”

On 5 June the second group of Daughters of Saint Anne embarked on the steamer Orénoque.

Destination: Bolivia, via Argentina.

An adventurous, very long journey lasting four months. They crossed the Andes by carriage on barely passable roads and arrived, exhausted, in Sucre in mid-August.

By 1884 there were already four foundations in Bolivia: La Paz, Sucre, Cochabamba and Oruro, with a flourishing novitiate. The Superior General decided to set up the American Province and appointed Sr A. Camilla Valentini Provincial.

A year later she invited her to come to Italy to report on the new province.

Buenos Aires to Genoa: two months on the steamer Adria.

In Genoa a grand welcome awaited her. A missionary, an evangelizer, had arrived.

“How beautiful,” says the Bible, “are the feet of those who bring good news of peace and good...”

At the Mother House the Provincial of America and her two companions passed between two rows of postulants holding lighted candles. All went to the chapel for a solemn Te Deum.

Sisters, priests, gentlemen and bishops wanted to see the returned missionaries and hear about the missions.

The following year, 1886, Sr A. Camilla Valentini set off again for America, taking fourteen more missionaries with her.

A poor Sister is an all-powerful Sister

Mother Rosa would never fulfill her dream of going to America to visit the missions, for reasons of government, health and age. She would be a missionary by prayer, authority and counsel.

She would always stay very close to her missionary daughters through many letters.

Particularly revealing is her correspondence with Sr A. Virginia Gaggi — an exuberant, restless, volcanic temperament.

But good, devout and capable. Mother Rosa sent her to Bolivia as Visitor.

There she found some disorder. She wanted to crush everything — sulphuric acid, the scalpel — not oil and wine on the wounds, as Jesus teaches.

Mother Rosa calmed her: “Your constant reproaches give me great pain. Not for my own sake, for I deserve much worse... but for the good God, who because of my little wisdom must receive displeasure from his spouses. O sweet Crucified, your virtue teaches me to suffer.”

Sr Virginia realized she had struck a false note. “Mother,” she replied, “I am sorry to have grieved your heart...”50

She asked forgiveness and declared herself ready to do whatever she was told. But her patience ran out before the end of the letter.

“Do you want me to speak plainly? Remove the Superiors, or I’m coming home...”

With unruffled gentleness Mother Rosa wrote to her again: “Dear Daughter, what am I to say? You tell me to change the Superiors and put good ones in; but what am I to answer? Only to pray, and have others pray hard, that God in his infinite mercy may set everything right...”

Great humility shines through this letter. “You ask my forgiveness: I give you not one pardon but a hundred. If Superiors say something, it is for your good and for no other reason. If I were a little better, you would surely have great graces. But... poor Daughters, you have the misfortune of a wretched Mother who is just as poor in everything — truly pitiable...”

In 1884 the first foundation was made in Brazil, in Pará.

After Bolivia and Brazil came Chile and Peru — there too, hospitals and schools. In ten years more than sixteen houses. When the Mother died, the congregation had 43 houses in America.

In Brazil too, as in Bolivia and everywhere, there was frightening poverty at first. But the Mother was pleased.

“When houses begin in poverty,” she wrote, “they prosper more and please our Mother Saint Anne.”51

The Mother’s eyes were fixed on the poverty of Bethlehem, Nazareth and Calvary. “What we have more than he did only shows how different we are from him” (Charles de Foucauld).

“A poor Sister is an all-powerful Sister” (Chevrier). “The weakness of human means is a source of strength: God is master of the impossible” (Charles de Foucauld).

Sisters today are the only Gospel much of the world reads

The congregation’s growth now called for a General Chapter, to take stock of the situation and set the pace for the road ahead.

On 17 May 1881 Cardinal Ferrieri wrote to Bishop Scalabrini of Piacenza: “In order to give the Superior General her General Council, whose consent is required under the Constitutions for deciding the most important matters concerning the Institute, you will, if you think fit, arrange for a regular General Chapter to be held, always according to the norms laid down in the oft-mentioned Constitutions.”

Bishop Scalabrini convened the General Chapter for August of that year in Piacenza.

Seventy-four Superiors attended.

It was preceded by a retreat for the Chapter members.

The preacher was the Rev. Mr Manzi, a Vincentian and Superior of the Alberoni College.

Mother Gattorno contributed with daily conferences, always on some point of the Rule.52

Those conferences have come down to us. Reading them, one finds a little treatise on the ascetical life for Superiors.

A few samples.

“A Superior must not have herself waited on.”

“Whoever commands must take less care of herself than whoever obeys.”

“For the love of God, give good example: be like a mirror of true observance, so that your sisters may copy every virtue from you.”

“Woe to the Superior who does not know better than anyone else how to rein in her own heart.”

Two quotations from modern authors show how timely these norms are.

The well-known moral theologian Bernhard Häring writes: “Unfortunately there are among... educators too many mere animal-tamers, drill-masters, who are satisfied with themselves and their subordinates only when they have achieved the result of training, that is, when by whatever method they have managed to impose an external order by coercion... The man of power in a position of command is always tempted to remain a tamer.”

The idea of the “mirror” is often stressed by Cardinal Suenens: “Sisters today are the only Gospel much of the world reads.”

Excuse me, Sister, but has your God died, by any chance?

More advice to Superiors.

“Always leave your Sisters complete freedom to write to the Mother General...” Speaking of this, a lump rose in her throat. She had suffered so much from certain indiscretions.

“Correct faults with motherly gentleness.”

One hears the mother. Give love to receive love. Love in order to call forth love.

We find love when we know how to give it.

“Provide your Sisters with wholesome reading.”

Note the call to provide books for the Sisters.

Mother Rosa did not fall under the excommunication of Fr Rétif, who writes in his book The Mission: “Superiors, men and women, have a grave duty to stock the library generously and renew it constantly; a part of the budget, however small, must be set aside for it. A young Franciscan friend of mine used to say that a Superior who did not buy five or six volumes of good spirituality or theology for the library every year would be in a state of mortal sin.”

Other advice Mother Rosa gave:

“Always be in good humor with your Sisters, covering with a cheerful face whatever pain you have in your heart.”

“At recreation stay with the Sisters as much as you can.”

Today we say it in grander words: “Educational effectiveness is directly proportional to knowledge of the person to be educated. The more I know, the more I can do.”

Presence and joy.

God alone knows how much need there is today too for an air of genuine joy to circulate in convents.

Meeting certain mournful faces, one is tempted to ask:

“Excuse me, Sister, but has your God died, by any chance?”

A rather well-known man was once asked why he had left religious life after only a short time.

His caustic reply: “It wasn’t the fasts, the vigils or the penances that made me flee the monastery: it was the recreations of those good Fathers.”

“Above all with sick Sisters, exquisite charity and generosity.”

“No stinginess with food. Poverty is not stinginess. Convents are not made to ruin people’s health.”

“Notice how you are being treated during these days of retreat. Do the same for your communities.”

Four hours in the waiting room

When the retreat was over, Bishop Scalabrini presided at the session of the General Chapter that was to vote on certain observations made by the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Religious regarding the Constitutions.

The whole Chapter unanimously declared itself opposed to these observations, judging them harmful to the Institute.

The Bishop pointed out that “a vote against the amendments might endanger or even delay the final approval of the Constitutions”; but since he did not advise them to vote again, the Chapter members did not realize how important the matter was.

The consequences are easy to imagine.

Cardinal Ferrieri at once summoned the Servant of God to Rome.

He received her on 3 December, after keeping her waiting four hours in the anteroom, from eight till noon.

“Your action looks for all the world like disobedience and rebellion against the Holy See.”

“Your Eminence, I confess I was a thousand miles from suspecting any disobedience in that vote...”

And she wanted to apologize.

But the Cardinal cut her short and dismissed her.

Rosa asked for help from Cardinal Alimonda, Protector of the Institute, who advised her to write the Sacred Congregation a letter of retraction.

The changes Rome wanted were made to the Constitutions, and the incident was settled.

Calm returned.

“... And now I have some splendid news for you... Tomorrow the Pope will receive all the Chapter members in audience.”53

Cardinal Alimonda, Protector of the Daughters of Saint Anne, had closed the third General Chapter by announcing the audience with the Holy Father. The third General Chapter had gathered 180 members from various parts of the world.

When Leo XIII saw that great throng of Sisters, he turned to the Mother General and said:

“Rosa, what have you done?”

“Nothing, Holy Father.”

Then the Pope stretched out his hand towards the crowd of Superiors and added: “You have prayed much, and this is the fruit of prayer. Persevere in prayer and in the observance of the Rules.”

“Holy Father, we ask a special blessing for our missions in Africa... there are several of them now.”

“Gladly... but do not be in a hurry for conversions. A little fruit each year, but solid. And for the missions too... prayer, prayer.”54

The third Chapter had been held in the autumn of 1888, when the foundation had already grown greatly.

In 1883 building had begun on the Generalate in Rome. The Sisters moved in in January 1886, and the house was blessed by His Holiness’s Cardinal Vicar on the 18th of that month. Beside the house stands the church, open to the public.

In the Generalate today rest the remains of Rosa Gattorno, which were exhumed from the Verano cemetery in 1932 and found incorrupt; there they await the glorification the Church is wont to give even on earth to God’s most valiant servants.

Rosa Gattorno would spend the last fourteen years of her life in this house on Via Merulana.

In the spring of 1885 the foundress was in Rome for Easter, and on that occasion had another audience with the Holy Father Leo XIII.

The Pope received her like a father. He questioned her at length about her work and was very pleased with what the Daughters of Saint Anne were doing in Italy and the world. Mother Rosa presented him with a booklet just published in Naples describing their works of charity in that city during the cholera of 1884.

The foundress came away from that audience “drunk with consolation”, as she wrote to one of her secretaries.

Her heart flooded with hope, she presented to the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars the text of the Constitutions amended along the lines of the observations repeatedly received in those years.

“Let’s hope this is it,” she said to herself. Unfortunately it was not yet.

On 30 August a letter from Cardinal Schiaffino informed her that the Constitutions were not only not definitively approved but were to be printed with the required changes and kept on trial for another ten years.

Final approval of the Constitutions would come only in 1892, the year of the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Mother Foundress’s clothing.

For the occasion every house sent a gift to the Mother Foundress at the Generalate in Rome, and an exhibition of these gifts was even set up in the Via Merulana premises.

But the finest gift on that day, 26 July 1892, was brought by the Cardinal Protector himself. That morning he came to the Generalate to celebrate Mass. Afterwards, as he left the chapel to be welcomed by the whole community lined up in the wide corridor, he had two Sisters go ahead of him, Sr A. Benedetta Carrega and Sr A. Celsa Speranza, carrying on a silver tray the book of the Constitutions with the papal decree of final approval, dated that very day, 26 July 1892.

With a smile the Cardinal handed that volume and that precious sheet to Mother Gattorno, who was the first to meet him at the chapel door. They were the seal of a long story, the reward of hard labor.

Intense emotion flooded the hearts of all the Sisters, and especially Mother Gattorno’s.

When on 10 November of the previous year she had asked the Cardinal for this great grace, she had ended by exclaiming: “Then I shall die happy!” Her prayer had been answered three years before the decade set by Cardinal Schiaffino.

The diary of that memorable day was written by Sr A. Celsa Speranza. To her we owe some details worth recording, for they reveal the Servant of God’s sensitivity.

When she held the approved Constitutions in her hands she was beside herself with joy. She ran off and hid on the first floor and even lost her crucifix. Sr A. Benedetta went looking for her but could not find her. When the Servant of God had regained her composure she went to His Eminence to thank him.

“It is not you who should thank me,” the Cardinal replied, “but the Church that should thank you. The Institute is no longer yours; it belongs to the Church.”

Her Daughters perform feats of charity

“Naples is utterly desolate; this disease is more plague than cholera. May God, Mary Most Holy and Saint Anne help this people! Your Daughters are performing feats of charity.”

So wrote Mgr Gennaro Di Belmonte, the future cardinal, from Naples in 1885.

That year cholera had swept Italy. Once again the Daughters of Saint Anne had the chance to live their vocation as witnesses of charity.

The disease at once took very violent forms. “The scourge advances so fast that anyone struck becomes a corpse at once,” Sr A. Martina wrote to the foundress from Naples on 10 September 1884. Within hours the contagion killed, leaving bodies blackened like coal.

Hygienic precautions were minimal. The population was literally terrified. Doctors and medicines were lacking.

“Yesterday,” Sr A. Martina writes again, “nearly a thousand new cases broke out — that’s no exaggeration — and the newspapers report only a third. The city is in great confusion: endless penitential processions; five have passed while I’ve been writing. Barefoot men, women with their hair let down... tonight I felt like weeping, seeing about two thousand people following the statue of Saint Anne, led by a hundred gentlemen with ropes round their necks and their hands tied.”

Mother Gattorno assigned all the Sisters she could spare to the cholera victims.

Under the direction of their Superior, Sr A. Martina, and with Mgr Di Belmonte’s spiritual and moral support, they did marvellous work.

“These Daughters of yours,” Monsignor wrote, “are no longer women but angels of charity. The whole Institute is surely sustained by the blessings these nurses receive... Mother, as soon as the cholera is over, you must come and comfort them with a visit.”

The foundress was present every day through her letters.

All the Sisters survived except one, Sr A. Adele. Just as the cholera was dying out in Naples towards the end of September, Sr A. Adele was struck so violently that within a few hours she was dead.

To the confessor who comforted her she answered: “And what are these sufferings compared with what Jesus suffered for me?”5556

The Daughters of Saint Anne not only nursed cholera patients in the isolation hospitals but went into homes as much as they could.

“The sick in their homes,” Mgr Di Belmonte wrote, “lock themselves in and will open neither to the mayor, nor the carabinieri, nor the priests — only to the nuns.”

“Your Daughters,” he said in another letter, “are adored for the way they serve the sick.”

But the most authoritative and precious praise came from Cardinal Sanfelice, Archbishop of Naples, who wrote to Mother Gattorno: “The work of your Sisters is truly edifying: they vie with one another in proofs of remarkable charity and have won ever more the reverence and love they deserve among the Neapolitans and beyond.”

The needs were so great that someone suggested sending the novices themselves to nurse the sick. A few somewhat scrupulous souls raised objections, but Mgr Di Belmonte took full responsibility: “On my responsibility I suspend the novitiate.”

When it came to their profession, Mgr Di Belmonte himself asked Rome for the necessary dispensations.

On 6 October 1884 he wrote to Mother Gattorno: “I am begging the Holy Father to allow all these novices to make their vows now as an exception, since in ten years one could not have greater proofs of vocation than these fine young women have given in two months.”

When cholera broke out in Liguria, the witness of charity of the Daughters of Saint Anne shone there too. A gentleman of that region wrote to Mother Gattorno in October 1884: “How many sworn enemies of nuns were forced on this occasion to admire and praise the acts of heroic self-denial of these Sisters! The whole town is truly edified. The most critical cannot understand how young cloistered women can find in themselves the courage to endure toil and face dangers before which even the strongest men sometimes feel helpless.”

In 1887 cholera raged in Sicily too. Of the work of the Daughters of Saint Anne on that occasion we quote just one testimony, that of Archbishop Guarino of Messina.

“These Daughters of yours are truly the charity of Jesus Christ made visible. May God keep and bless them. I see them everywhere — placid, ready, hard-working, calm... their virtue must be great.

“How can one not love and bless them in the Lord from the depths of one’s soul? Even people who give little thought to God admire their self-denial, their charity, their cheerfulness at work... Rejoice in it, Mother, as I do with all my heart, all the more because the whole city esteems and venerates them.”

In East Africa

On 5 September 1885 Mother Gattorno received from the Italian Foreign Ministry a request for two Sisters for the hospital at Assab. It was the first time Italy had asked for a women’s order for its colony.

The negotiations took about a year. The foundress secured that not two but four Sisters be sent, and insisted that there be priests for their spiritual care. Three Capuchin Fathers were assigned.57

The Sisters’ work was teaching; later the hospital would come too. Unfortunately slavery still reigned among the Africans, and many children were abandoned. The Daughters of Saint Anne at Assab sought out abandoned newborns and ransomed slaves when they could. It was work bristling with difficulties. For a long time, when the Capuchin Father who looked after them was gone, they were deprived of all religious support — whole months without Communion. The Mother made herself present through many letters, all overflowing with encouragement and motherly care.

“Well done! Your zeal and your labors will crown you with precious pearls.”

“May God keep you a thousand years for the good of Africa.”

“My God, how sad not to have Sisters! I wish I were ten years younger... I would come and be your cobbler, but I am very old and always in very poor health.”

“How sad for me not to have Sisters! It’s a real scourge, because the novitiates are full but they aren’t ready.”

In 1894 Leo XIII established the Apostolic Prefecture of Eritrea, entrusting it to Fr Michele da Carbonara.

From then on the Daughters of Saint Anne had a free field for all their apostolic work in Eritrea.

General Baratieri wrote to Mother Gattorno in September of that year: “I am always glad when I can be of service to the Daughters of Saint Anne... for the good they do in the Colony... I am ready to give up a wing of my villa to house the Sisters, who have served religion and humanity so well.”58

Everything seemed to be going well when suddenly the Italo-Abyssinian war broke out.

The disastrous outcome of that very brief conflict is well known. Once the painful episode was over, ordinary life resumed in Eritrea and the Daughters of Saint Anne multiplied their missionary works.

The new Visitor, Sr A. Gerarda Canovi, who served as Superior of the whole mission, fully shared the Servant of God’s outlook. In every letter the Mother had nothing but praise for her work.

“Surely the local people will marvel at your sacrifice among them in those lands... But sacrifice alone beautifies our soul and makes it great in the Lord’s sight. Here, then, are more Christian souls: how fortunate you are in so fine a mission.”

“I am delighted with the good news you give me of the Sisters.”

“A line in answer to yours, to show you that I always reply... just one line because I am very ill; but I’m afraid that if you saw someone else’s handwriting it would upset you.”

As long as she could, Mother Gattorno wrote to her Daughters herself. She would write even on her deathbed.

Her last letter to Sr A. Canovi is dated 30 April 1900 and is the only one dictated, since Rosa could no longer write. It has all the tenderness and solemnity of an apostolic testament.

“I was deeply grateful for your lovely letter, and I assure you it pains me to hand over the pen to have someone else reply; but I am forced to, because the swelling and breathlessness have made me very ill and I am in a pitiful state.

“Pray, for charity’s sake, and have others pray...

“I commend to you the holy observance of the Rules: the Superior must be the lighthouse guiding everyone to a safe harbor...

“If you did not receive a letter from me on Holy Thursday, receive it today, and in it I repeat what dear Jesus suggested to my heart. Look after the interests of your heavenly Spouse; win souls for him.”

Her last words to a missionary Superior reveal the dream of her whole religious life.

The finest flower of the missionary work of the Daughters of Saint Anne in Eritrea would be Mgr Chidanè-Mariam Cassa, the first native bishop of Eritrea.

On 24 July 1937 he wrote to the then Mother General, Sr A. Corredentrice Pomarici, on her fiftieth anniversary of religious life: “Almost 50 per cent of the young people who make up, one may say, the new generation of Catholics have passed through the schools of the Daughters of Saint Anne... And the dear Sisters... can be proud to count many of their former pupils among our priests.”

At this point the reader will be wondering: “And what became of Rosa Gattorno’s children, Alessandro and Carlotta?”

Alessandro was at boarding school from nine to eighteen — first in Genoa, then Savona, then Mondovì, and finally Novi Ligure — but unfortunately nothing good came of it. Having failed in his studies, he took it into his head to go into trade.

So Mother Rosa took him out of school and placed him with relatives in Genoa so that he could learn the rudiments of business.

But at twenty-one he wanted to try his luck in America. Those were the years when many Italians emigrated to America, lured by the mirage of easy fortune. Fr Accinelli himself and his uncle Federico advised Alessandro to go. Before leaving he went to Piacenza to say goodbye to his mother.

For Rosa that embrace tasted of death — not so much bodily as spiritual death. She writes in her Memoirs: “Surely my son would die without the comforts of Holy Church and not as a good Christian, and then I would have lost him for eternity. Shall a creature who belongs to me not die in the kiss of my God?... I cannot bear such pain. O my Love, let him suffer a thousand deaths, let him see them, but as a Christian!”

Her eyes clouded [?] with tears. Then suddenly a thought flashed into her mind and she made a solemn promise: “My Love, I promise you that if I have the grace of seeing him die as a Christian I will not shed a tear, but will drink down that sorrow from your most holy hands, happy to be able to give him to you, so that he may be yours for eternity.”

The American venture too was a failure. Alessandro stayed in America barely a year. He kept writing home asking his poor mother for more money. And unfortunately the failure was not only material but moral too.

One of his letters also reveals the origin, the first impulse, of his moral and religious straying.

“I have changed a great deal more in my religious ideas,” he wrote to his mother, “and I’ll tell you how. You must know that since I was a boy, hearing people talk of Federico (his Garibaldian uncle), and then seeing how fond he was of my family and still is... I had made him my master and wanted to follow in his footsteps. But now I realize his steps are false, and the whole world can see it; so, if God allows me, I shall leave the beaten track and try to make good the harm done.”

Excellent resolutions — but sadly short-lived!

“I am not a Christian,” writes Guéhenno. “To become one I would need to stumble upon a Christian.”5960

Alessandro, weak-willed as he was, needed to stumble upon an uncle who was a Christian. Unfortunately his uncle openly professed anticlericalism and, what is more, had been living openly with a woman for two years without marrying her. Following that example, the nephew too slid down the path of scandal.

In Florence, where he had found work in a bank, he fell in love with a girl of doubtful virtue. After a while he pretended he had to marry her, to wring from his mother her consent to the marriage. Or did he want, yet again, to cadge some money from her?

The wedding took place in Rome in the spring of 1879. Dismissed once more by the bank, Alessandro and his wife ended up being taken in by Mother Gattorno, who gave him some work on the Gargatano estate near Piacenza.

On 21 November 1890 the Servant of God was in Rome when a telegram from Bishop Scalabrini told her that her son Alessandro was seriously ill. He died on 16 March 1891, attended by two priests who for a long time had never left him, day or night. Mother Rosa kept her promise. Though torn with grief, she did not let a single tear escape.

But she would write in her Memoirs: “Only my God knew what it cost me and what I suffered.”

Fr Fiocchi relates: “From seven in the morning until five in the afternoon (the hour of death) Mother Gattorno sat motionless beside her dying son, praying in agony of soul that eternal life might at last be assured to that son of her tears. As the shadows of the winter evening wrapped the misty city... Alessandro breathed his last. Then the devout mother rose dry-eyed, just as she had promised sixteen years before, and gave instructions for the body; then she withdrew to the house on Via Farnese... shut herself in her room and gave vent to her grief. For about two hours they heard her sobbing from outside.”

The next day, while Alessandro’s funeral was being held in the cathedral, Bishop Scalabrini was handing the mission crucifix, in the chapel of the Mother House, to six Daughters of Saint Anne who would sail for New York a few days later.

Another very sharp thorn in Mother Gattorno’s life was her daughter Carlotta.

In 1873 Count Gaspare Barbiellini asked for her hand. Everyone was against the match, but the couple insisted. They were married in Genoa in the spring of 1876 and settled in Piacenza, where several children were born to them. But troubles soon began that embittered the poor Mother for more than twenty years. Her son-in-law claimed rights over property that actually belonged to the Institute. Mother Gattorno was inflexible: she would not yield a pin of what belonged to the Institute. Daughter and son-in-law appealed to influential people, in vain. When conscience was involved, Mother Gattorno would not give an inch.

Some of her Daughters, unwisely listening to tendentious rumors, went so far as to provoke an inquiry from Rome. Though in the end it all only made the Servant of God’s integrity shine more brightly, the storm was long; seven years later it would bring about an Apostolic Visitation, one of the last and most painful trials in Mother Gattorno’s embattled life.

I want to be with you until death

In Rome Princess Odescalchi, whenever she met a Daughter of Saint Anne, used to say: “How is your Crucified One?... Your Mother really is crucified.”

Toil, suffering and penance had truly crucified her. In 1894, on doctor’s orders, she had to accept eggs, dairy products and a little wine.

As for rest... she was not easily persuaded. Indeed in 1894 alone the congregation opened nineteen new houses.

Golden years for missionary vocations: from 1895 to 1900 between thirty and forty Sisters left each year for Africa and America. In Italy alone there were three novitiates, with seventy to ninety novices.

In 1896 a house for nursing the sick was opened in Barcelona, Spain.

In the spring of 1898 the Mother set out on her last journey to Sicily. The Sisters in the secretariat appealed to the Cardinal Protector to dissuade her from so tiring a journey, but the Cardinal replied: “The Mother’s sufferings are not ordinary ones, so I don’t feel I can stand in her way.”

On 10 April she spoke to all the Superiors of the island gathered in Palermo. She seemed to sense she would not see them again. Among other things she told them: “When you kiss the crucifix, say: Lord, I want to be with you until death. Before you sleep: Lord, give me holy perseverance.”

She returned to Rome at the end of May. The effects of the exhausting journey were soon felt: prostration, breathlessness, extreme weakness of the heart. The doctor advised her to leave Rome, and she went to Piacenza. There a new trial awaited her: the sudden arrival of Abbot Domenico Serafini as Apostolic Visitor, who reached the Mother House at two in the afternoon on 28 July. This visitation was the result of her son-in-law’s unjust claims and the petty campaign of insinuations, suspicions and accusations that grew out of them.

It is easy to imagine the Mother’s anguish at this new danger hanging over her work.

“And yet,” she would sometimes say with a sigh, as if concluding a long speech locked in her heart, “and yet I have had no other aim in my work than the glory of God.”

On 30 August, her name day, the Sisters and novices of Piacenza held a little celebration for her.

On that occasion she spoke words that have all the flavor of a spiritual testament.

“Hold fast to the holy Rule; love the holy Institute; do not be like those who make excuses because of slanders or hard work, and so say they can no longer stay in the Institute, and stop serving the Lord to go to an earthly creature. Who is better than the Lord? Is it not better to serve the Creator than the creature?

“Look at the crucifix when trials assail you: who suffered more than he?”

The crucifix: the norm, the secret, the root of everything.

Her last days in Piacenza were marked by keen pain at the Apostolic Visitor’s presence. She was sustained by the hope that the Lord would guide everything for the greater good of the Institute.

From this period — mid-October — comes a particularly important talk to the novices, because it sums up the main lines of the spirituality that should mark the Daughter of Saint Anne. In it echo the most essential themes of religious life:

“I leave you a keepsake, my daughters: the love of God! Not a languid love, but love, true love. A word hard to understand: not cold, sterile love, but the true love a spouse of Jesus Christ must have. St Teresa used to say: whoever loves does not offend the beloved.”

“...You are in the novitiate to learn to meditate well...”

“...A religious must always think of Jesus, love him, be wholly his... How beautiful to be completely detached from relatives, from Superiors, from that patient, from the confessor...”

On 20 November 1898 Mother Gattorno climbed for the last time to her mysterious little room. She prayed there a long time and then closed it. She would never enter it again. Later her Daughters would enter it, and visitors who would linger there in prayer.6162

I have finished suffering

“I think Saint Anne wanted this thanksgiving feast from me because it may be the last I keep on earth.”

She sensed her end was near. That is why she wanted the feast of Saint Anne in 1899 to be especially solemn. The last six months of that year were a painful pilgrimage from house to house in search of air that might give her a little health: Tuscany, Liguria, Piedmont. In Genoa, at the house of S. Silvestro, a violent heart attack lasting several hours struck on 12 October. As soon as she recovered she was taken to Rome, accompanied by Professor Lupi, her brother Francesco and some Sisters.

In Rome she rallied somewhat. In November and December she still attended to various very important affairs of the Institute, and wrote, entirely in her own hand, a very clear will to protect her congregation’s property from all harassment. The document is dated 20 November 1899.

On the 26th of that month she had the great consolation of seeing the great friend and benefactor of the Daughters of Saint Anne, His Excellency Mgr Gennaro Granito Pignatelli Di Belmonte, newly appointed Apostolic Nuncio in Brussels, consecrated bishop.

On 10 February 1900 the Mother was struck down by a severe bout of influenza. Her heart was in such a state that the worst was expected. Because of swelling throughout her body she could not even stay in bed. She spent most of the day sitting on a chair, but constantly refused any armchair or chair with arms. She dozed for long hours, but as soon as she opened her eyes she turned them to the crucifix.

When a little strength returned she would write letters to distant Superiors. Her last letter in her own hand is dated 1 May 1900.

As her abdomen swelled more and more, she decided to ask her faithful Sr A. Serafina Foglia for a particularly delicate service. She trusted Sr A. Serafina greatly, knowing her simplicity, and turned to her for small services; she liked to pray at length with her; for three months now this Sister had not left her day or night.

Very gently, Sr A. Serafina set about removing from her waist the chain the Servant of God had fastened there forty-two years before and had never taken off. But she could not undo it, because the joining link had been closed. She had to take a strong pair of pincers to break a link. With the chain came shreds of flesh which, from adhering so many years and from the recent swelling, had become caught in it.

On 4 May Mother Rosa said to the Sisters around her: “Now I have finished suffering: everything has been averted.” She meant the storms that had beaten upon the Institute, which she now considered dispelled.

That evening she received Communion as Viaticum. Her mind was perfectly clear; her will had kept all its strength. Even on the eve of her death she found the strength to get out of bed and pray for a few moments before Our Lady.

She got back into bed with extreme difficulty and stammered with effort: “Now I won’t get up again.” These were the last words she spoke clearly. Fr Vincenzo da Alatri, a Capuchin, her confessor, gave her Extreme Unction and the apostolic blessing.

The next morning, 6 May 1900, she died.

The Sisters who performed the last services for her venerated body found many scars, healed for some time. Around her waist many red wounds showed, made by various instruments of penance.

Wounds crying out her love for the Lord. Wounds that were the trophy of a battle lasting more than forty years, a battle fought to witness to her love for Christ Crucified. “I did not love you in jest!” Christ had said to Angela of Foligno in one of her overwhelming inner communications. Six centuries later, with the bloody eloquence of her wounds, Rosa Gattorno could repeat the same cry to the Spouse of her soul: “I have not loved you in jest.”

A modern author has a very striking image: I think, he says, that the Lord keeps in heaven a splendidly illustrated edition of the Gospel which he guards jealously. He updates it constantly, every hour.

On one side is the text — his words, his teachings. On the other, the illustrations. Not those of great artists; they do not interest him. The illustrations are supplied daily from earth by people who cannot hold a paintbrush but who know how to take his teaching seriously. The Gospel illustrated by the saints — above all by millions of unknown saints — grows beyond measure.

On one side the words of Christ; on the other the “deeds” of men.

On one side his teaching; on the other its practical interpretation.

It is an immense, boundless volume. The Lord looks at it with pleasure every moment. That Gospel, commented on and illustrated by deeds, shows him that his visit to earth was not in vain.

This edition of the Gospel includes Rosa Gattorno’s illustrations too.

In this and the next two chapters we shall see how she illustrated what Jesus said and did regarding the three theological virtues of faith, hope and charity.

Rosa Gattorno often confessed that God had given her the gift of a deep, firm faith: “God,” she said, “set my faith in diamond.”

And only a woman as full of faith as she was could face all the obstacles that stood in the way of her work.

First of all, the sacrifice of her children — a necessary condition for saying yes to her vocation.

Every “yes” to a divine call presupposes a total act of faith. And every act of faith is an act of love made by closing one’s eyes to the narrow view of the earthly horizon in order to open them on the boundless immensity of a promise that, canceling time and space, seems to take from the creature every most natural and necessary support.

But how Rosa Gattorno had to close her eyes before her two tender children, already tried by death, illness and human injustice!

“Holy Father, I have two small children,” she would cry, weeping bitterly, to Pope Pius IX on 3 January 1866. “I love them too much; I cannot leave them; it is impossible.” And after the Pontiff’s stern command she would carry her anguish to the feet of Our Lady of Sorrows in the Servite church: “My children! I don’t know how to find the strength to leave them! And where? And with whom?”

A mother’s tortured heart was speaking to another heart that had known the supreme martyrdom of motherhood. She was heard and understood: “Absorbed in prayer,” Rosa continues in her Memoirs, “I found myself transformed... Generously I made my offering to God, repeating Abraham’s words: here I am to do your will... I will not complain again... and the Blessed Virgin assured me (inwardly) that she would keep my children as her own.”63

“Abraham’s words”... But God tested Abraham’s faith only once, by asking for his son’s life — his physical life only. Rosa had to endure, one might say day by day for many long years, in a renewed act of faith in the fulfilment of the promise, the anguish of her son’s spiritual death, until her heroic resolve: “... If I have the grace of seeing him die as a Christian, I will not shed a tear...”

But before that: “How often I was tempted to abandon everything and go back to my children; but I always repeated to myself the words the Holy Father Pius IX said to me; and the thought of acting against God’s will made me resist every martyrdom, and I repeated those words: ‘You will have no peace for the rest of your life.’ What words! And spoken by the Holy Father, so seriously!”

“Spoken by the Holy Father.” An act of faith more valid and solid than any other: faith in God, recognized not in the possible illusion of a pseudo-mystical impulse but in the unmistakable command of his Vicar, whom she had dared to ask — with a boldness only a mother’s desperation could explain and justify — for the seal of her vocation. And God, through the Pope’s mouth, had told her: “God will take care of your children; you take care of God in his Work.”64

Rosa believed; but she felt she was dying: “I felt my breast breaking.”

This inhuman anguish of Rosa Gattorno’s heart must be stressed once more to grasp the scope of the superhuman act of faith with which, on the strength of a divine promise but with such slender human guarantees, she accepted her mission of spiritual motherhood.

Abraham comes to mind again: “Go from your country and your kindred and your father’s house to the land that I will show you” (Gen 12:1).

It would have been much easier and more reassuring to rely on the church authorities in Genoa, who were not only well disposed but ready to take on the future work as their own; to keep a door open behind her — her father’s house — in case of failure; to be able to keep closer to her children (“leave them! And where? And with whom?”).

But Rosa understood that God wanted her in Piacenza, and though she did not move until she had obtained the Archbishop of Genoa’s permission and blessing, to Piacenza she went.

In the first months — months of very harsh poverty and arid loneliness in an unfamiliar town, more inclined to look on curiously and gossip than to come forward with real help and Christian understanding — three of her first five companions left her. “The time will come,” Rosa remarked unperturbed, “when these rooms will not be enough to hold all the companions who will want to join us.”

The political situation was highly unfavorable to the foundation: “The Masonic press raised loud protests because the newly arrived nuns were evading (and implicitly mocking) the law suppressing religious congregations.”

One day a priest came and said to her: “What are you doing here? Shut up shop and send them all home — that’s best.” But Rosa Gattorno answered simply that she feared no obstacle; her work was God’s work and so it would go on: Pius IX himself had assured her of it.

The spite of enemies, one can bear; but the misunderstanding of good people!

This cup too Rosa had to drain to the dregs. But she did not turn back, nor would she.

“Our faith is Someone,” wrote François Mauriac. Rosa Gattorno’s faith was Jesus Crucified.

She invariably ended her letters with the words: “I hold you close in my Crucified.”

When she gave advice she would end by saying: “Go, run to your Crucified, and if you have faith you will infallibly obtain it.”

“My Crucified,” she said, “will see to everything. My Crucified will guard his Work.”

She would have been happy to shed her blood for the faith: “Oh, if only I were granted,” she was heard to exclaim more than once, “to shed my blood for the faith!”

“How I would love to die a martyr, to purge my sins and see Jesus soon.”

But her faith shone out in her life even more than in her words.

For her, setting an example was a demand of faith.

“Remember,” she told Superiors, “that we are like the crucifix on the altar in full view of all the faithful, so we must not let the Sisters see any fault in us. The Superior is like a lampstand that must give light to all.”6566

The wind of words does not bring subjects to their knees; it is example that draws them. There are Superiors who have no need to speak; it is enough that they are present. Their presence is already a call. A true Superior does us good just by our looking at them.

A born Superior, Rosa always showed humble faith and religious veneration towards her own Superiors, beginning of course with the Supreme Pontiff.

Her delicate sensitivity towards the supreme authority of the Church is all the more significant because she must surely have been aware of the very grave problems then troubling the consciences of Italians, Catholic and non-Catholic. With her quick intelligence and soul open to life, the discussions she had not only heard in her youth but, as her brothers testify, taken part in, must have made her understand the serious, profound reasons “the other side” put forward for its imperious demand for Rome as the capital of Italy — even amid the tangle of errors and resentments mixed with those good reasons, which exploded in the blind accusations of Masonic atheism.

But her Christian conscience, above rather than aloof from political circumstances, knew how to combine affectionate understanding for those in error (her brothers and many others dear to her were in error) with the most devoted fidelity to the Apostolic See; and, leaping over every ground of controversy, she came swiftly to the conclusion dictated by faith: “Let the Daughters of Saint Anne,” we read in the Constitutions — not written by her but certainly inspired by her — “ask for the grace always to be united with the infallible Head of the Church, the Supreme Pontiff...”67

Nor would she tolerate criticism of the Pope in her presence, from anyone. A Catholic must see Jesus in him and accept his unquestionable authority in matters of faith. Everything else was none of her concern.

Notable was her devotion to the “dear” Eternal Father, as she used to call him. She even wanted the month of January to be dedicated in the Institute to special devotion in his honor.

Her faith in the efficacy of the sacraments was very lively. To Daughters who confided spiritual troubles to her she invariably recommended Communion:

“Communion! My dear, for pity’s sake, don’t stay away from this fountain of grace!”

“My daughter, I urge you to receive Holy Communion; your coldness, which wants to keep away from so immense a treasure, frightens me...”

Her devotion to Our Lady, particularly tender and trusting, bore every mark of authentic faith, just as she showed she understood the deep theological basis of devotion to Saint Anne, whom she never named without adding: “Mother of the Immaculate”.

But one may say that her spirit of faith took on a poetic glow when she expressed it in the concrete form of works of charity: her letters to her Daughters are full of phrases in which her Christ Crucified, the beloved object of her faith, is explicitly identified with the poor, suffering, humiliated brother.

“... Let us hope that good Jesus will deign to let himself be nursed by the poor daughters of Saint Anne...”

“... Take comfort, you who toil for your Jesus, for in touching the sick with charity... you touch Jesus who is in them.”

“Dear Daughters of Saint Anne, love, love Jesus. Make yourselves victims of charity. I envy you.”

“... You always have a way to meditate, seeing Jesus in the sick.”

Another expression of her faith was fundamental uprightness: “Let truth be your treasure, always,” she wrote to a Sister. And to a community: “Every action of ours... done solely for love of him will always please the Eternal Father. Let us see creatures in him and love them.”

And again: “May God’s will be done in us; that is all I wish to have.” So the spirit of faith was to be the spring that drove her daughters to work — not vanity or ambition.68

That woman is more up there than down here

When a soul lives by faith, the faith shows outwardly. True faith is always contagious. People who came into contact with Mother Gattorno came away full of admiration, saying things like: “That woman is more up there than down here.”

Hence the irresistible attraction she held for the young women who came to her for advice. Many Daughters of Saint Anne confess that they owe their decision to consecrate themselves to God to their conversations with Mother Gattorno.

They wrote to her: “After our conversation I can no longer resist. I feel the Lord wants me in your Institute.”

The irresistible attraction of a faith that radiated far beyond her humble manner! An attraction unwittingly heightened by another shining proof of the authenticity of Rosa Gattorno’s faith: her spirit of poverty. For there is no authentic faith without the seal of a poverty that joyfully stretches the free and naked soul towards him who “clothes the lilies of the field and feeds the birds of the air” (Lk 12:24,27).

For Mother Rosa the love of poverty was a true cult. Anyone entering her little room in Piacenza receives a real shock.

That iron bedstead, that mattress of maize leaves laid on boards, that straw pillow... no proper mattress, no sheets... for more than twenty years she slept there fully dressed, wrapped in two black shawls. That was all the furniture that was to be prepared for her in the houses she visited. She brought the two shawls with her.

Poverty in dress: her habit was always spotless but worn and often patched. One day she was given a new apron. She called Sr A. Celsa Speranza and said: “Give it to the cook to wear for a while; afterwards I’ll wear it.”

Poverty of spirit above all: “Come, let us leave these earthly things,” she wrote to her Daughters in a circular letter of 15 June 1894. “Let us raise our minds on high and try to have and desire those goods that God alone can give... the only ones we shall possess for eternity.”69

Fr Lebret used to pray:

“I am considered a good Christian... and now, rereading the Gospel, I have been seized with disquiet. St Luke’s ‘woe to you that are rich’ keeps ringing in my ears. My wealth is like a wall between you and me, like a moat between me and humanity. O God, free me from my riches!”

At the end of her life Rosa Gattorno, forcing her humility, could have said that there was no “wall” between God and her; the pure nakedness of faith had demolished every obstacle.

And across the “moat” that might have separated her from humanity, her charity had thrown a bridge over which her Daughters would go on passing in search of every misery and every sorrow.

Once upon a time there was a priest who preached on the hope and mercy of the good God. He reassured others while he himself despaired. After the sermon a young man came up and said: “Father, I would like to go to confession.”

The priest said he would hear his confession at once. In the confessional the young man declared his sins and then added:

“Father, I have done so much evil; I am lost.”

“What are you saying, my son? One must never despair.”

“Father, you don’t want me to despair; and what about you?”

It was like a ray of light: the astonished priest put away the thought of despair, became a religious and turned into a great saint. The good God had sent him an angel in the guise of a young man to show him that one must never despair.

The holy Curé of Ars loved this story and used to comment: “My children, there is so little faith in the world today that people either hope too much or despair.”

Mother Rosa hoped neither too much nor too little: she had true, authentic theological hope. Amid all her difficulties her trust in the Lord never failed.

Her lofty serenity amid so much business amazed people. “Sometimes,” Mother Celsa Speranza relates, “looking at the difficulties the Institute was in during my first years in the secretariat, I said to the Servant of God: ‘But Mother, you can’t possibly sleep when you go to bed!’ ‘Oh no, my daughter,’ she replied. ‘When I go to my room at night I think for two minutes, then I turn to my crucifix and say: I have done all I could, as best I could; now you take care of your Work. And then I lay everything at the feet of my crucifix and think no more about it, as if the Work did not exist.’ And I heard her say the same to several Superiors.”

“Several times,” another Sister says, “seeing her attacked on all sides and even betrayed by people she had helped, I asked her how she could still trust the human race; and the Servant of God answered: ‘I trust my Jesus, and that is enough.’”

As she felt, so she taught. To those who came to her in the most difficult situations she recommended first of all to let go of their own will and put themselves in the Lord’s hands as useless instruments, expecting every good from him. “Try to bring everything to the feet of Jesus Crucified: he will set everything right and give you peace and comfort in the adversities of this life.” “The less we put of our own, the more of God we shall find; working for the earth, only the earth will gather the fruits, and they will never be good for the Lord.”

The difficulties she met, especially in the early days of the foundation, convinced her that it was God’s work; and she was often heard to say: “If I saw the Institute sailing along smoothly I would be afraid, because it would seem to me not to be the Lord’s work.”

In those times of distress her way of praying and getting others to pray took on special fervor. She had the Blessed Sacrament exposed and sent the Sisters in turns to adoration.

She herself spent long hours in the chapel, setting every care aside. But from a phrase that once escaped her at the bedside of a seriously ill Sister, we know that in difficult cases she added particularly harsh penances to her prayers. “When a grace is hard to obtain,” she said, “I offer the Lord something very painful, and after that he has never refused me what I asked.”

In the spring of 1898, on her last journey to Sicily, she had taken her granddaughter Maria Barbiellini with her. In Palermo the girl fell seriously ill. Mother Gattorno called the doctor, who said the illness was grave.

Mother Gattorno spent the whole night praying before the Blessed Sacrament. Thinking she was alone, she prayed aloud. Towards morning she got up and left the chapel serene. She felt her prayer had been heard, and so it was: her granddaughter recovered.70717273

It is not the road that is impossible; it is the impossible that becomes a road

In 1891 she sent Sr A. Camilla Valentini as Superior to Bassano, telling her: “I’m sending you to a poor house; but if you have faith, Providence will not fail you.”

The Sister found the house in a disastrous state, lacking everything. So she thought of writing to Mother Rosa for help.

By way of reply the Mother, instead of sending money, sent her one more little girl to feed. “She’s three years old and has been warmly recommended to me; bring her up well for me, for in time she will bear fruit.”

The Sister understood. She set to work, mobilizing the girls and Sisters in a real crusade of prayer. Providence came. Sr Camilla was able to meet her needs and even renovate and enlarge the house. In the end she had to ask forgiveness not only of the Lord but also of the Mother for having lacked trust in the good God.

Woman of little faith, why did you doubt? Where there is hope, “it is not the road that is impossible; it is the impossible that becomes a road” (Evdokimov).

Only a woman of great faith and great hope could withstand, as she did for many years, the gusts of adversity with such wonderful greatness of soul.

Her never losing heart, her calm goodness and freshness throughout her government while fighting every kind of enemy and snare, were the fruit of a mysterious inner strength drawn from the deep certainty of God’s help, because she served him with simplicity of heart. In the solemn testimonies of the Processes judgments like this recur constantly: “I have never seen a soul so resigned to the Lord’s will as our Mother. We were often amazed to see how calmly she bore, I won’t say physical sufferings, which she took no account of at all, but moral sufferings too, of which there were so many.”7475

“To live in hope means to live in poverty, possessing nothing. And yet if we abandon ourselves to the economy of Divine Providence, we have all that we hope for. By faith we know God without seeing him; by hope we possess him without feeling his presence. If we hope in him, we already possess him, for hope is a confidence he creates in our souls as secret testimony that he has taken possession of us. So the soul that hopes in God already belongs to him, and to belong to him is the same as to possess him, for he gives himself completely to those who give themselves to him.

“Hope deprives us of everything that is not God, so that all things can serve their true purpose as means of bringing us to God.

“Hope is proportionate to detachment. It brings our souls to the state of most perfect detachment and in so doing restores all values, giving each its proper place. Hope empties our hands so that we can use them for work: it shows us that there is something worth working for, and teaches us how to do it.

“Without hope our faith gives us only a superficial knowledge of God. Without love and hope, faith limits us to knowing God as a stranger; for it is hope that throws us into the arms of his mercy and providence. If we hope in him we shall come not only to know that he is merciful but to experience his mercy in our lives.

“If, instead of trusting in God, I trust only in my own intelligence, strength and prudence, the means God has given me to find the way to him will all fail me. No created thing can really be of use to us without hope. To put one’s trust in visible things is to live in despair” (Thomas Merton).

The episode of Sr Camilla we have just told shows how Mother Rosa formed her Sisters. She did not want them small, petty, cut to the measure of merely natural virtues. She wanted them not to fear God’s leap.

“Men afraid of the leap: that is what we have become, men trained to mistrust the leap. Everyone passes by, and we stay on the edge of the abysses of the future” (Mounier).

Mother Gattorno would gladly have signed these lines Mounier wrote to a pupil: “Hoist the mainsail on the mainmast and, leaving the harbors where you vegetate, set sail for the farthest star, heedless of the night around you.”

We appoint you general for life

Mother Rosa’s hope was rooted in her deep humility.

“Are you thinking of raising a tall building? First see to the foundation of humility” (St Augustine).

The Servant of God often relates in her writings that in prayer she received precious lessons on humility as the condition for possessing the kingdom of God. “He made me understand how much he loves this beautiful virtue, and that one may have all the greatest qualities in the world, but without humility one cannot possess his kingdom.”

Sr Vincenza, full of veneration for the Mother, had begun secretly noting down all the events that seemed most extraordinary to her.

One day Mother Rosa discovered the manuscript. “What’s got into your head?” she said crossly, and burned the pages at once.

Everyone who met her was edified by her humility.

“Your Mother is holy because of her great humility,” the Franciscan Brother Angelo told a Daughter of Saint Anne. Visiting the Sicilian houses one year, she called on Cardinal Dusmet in Catania and had a long and rather stormy conversation with him, which ended with the Daughters of Saint Anne withdrawing from one house.

But the holy prelate was amazed at the Servant of God’s bearing.

“I was edified,” he later told the Provincial, Sr A. Battistina Bertuzzi, “by your Mother’s humility and submission: for however much I said to her, she took it all in holy peace.”

Not only did she not want to be called General; she tried several times to resign the generalate.7677

Word of her insistence eventually reached Leo XIII. In an audience granted to her together with Mother Carrega, the Pope talked her out of the idea and said: “No, no — on the contrary, we appoint you general for life.”

In one of his writings Jean Anouilh sets out his idea of the Last Judgment.

The righteous are at the gate of Paradise, a dense crowd in a hurry to get in, sure they have reserved seats, tense, bursting with impatience. Suddenly a murmur spreads among them: “It seems he forgives the others too!”

For a moment amazement leaves them motionless and dumb. Then come stunned looks, sighs, shouts, protests. They are indignant. “Was it worth it...” “If I’d known...” Their bile rises. Curses against God explode... And at that instant they are damned.

The judgment is made: they have judged themselves, excommunicated themselves.

Love has shown itself, and they have refused to know it.

Christianity is accepting love, letting love invade the heart. Christianity is love.

How did Mother Rosa Gattorno live the love of God and neighbor?

Her whole life is already a record of her love.

But we want to look more closely at this aspect of her spirituality.

The first, fundamental demand of love is to avoid offending the beloved: to avoid sin and help others avoid it, for sin is the greatest offense against God.

“If I knew that sin had entered the Lord’s Work (her Institute), I would die of grief.”

She understood venial faults, which are often due more to frailty than to malice.

But she could not understand grave sin in one of her Sisters.

“She was so distressed,” a Sister says, “when she learned that in some house backbiting was not avoided.”78

The devil too is chaste

Chastity was the fruit of her love for the Lord.

She lived it with great delicacy.

Extreme reserve in dealing with men. Great modesty about her own body — so much that for many years she suffered from a hidden ailment without ever submitting to a medical examination. An exaggeration, we say.

But the saints are all a little given to exaggeration.

Whoever loves always loves too much.

“... Because of the great love with which God loved us...” (St Paul).

But she spoke little of chastity. She did not want to give the impression that chastity was the first virtue.

She would have signed with both hands these words of Canon Jacques Leclercq:

“Of course chastity is a virtue, but it is not the virtue. Nor even the fair virtue. If there is a virtue we can call the fair virtue, it must be charity. It must be so, or else the Gospel is false.

“Yes! We must practice chastity and many other virtues. But one can also go to hell practicing chastity. The devil is chaste! So chastity must be practiced, but kept in its place. And chastity is like all the other virtues: first of all one must love it.”

Another face of her love for God: her spirit of mortification. She hardly ever ate meat — and yet from childhood she had been very fond of cured meats. But those were precisely what she gave up for the rest of her life.

“Mother, you overdo your penances!”

“It isn’t penance; it’s for health reasons”...

A memory of this fervor survives in the customs of the Daughters of Saint Anne, who give up fruit on the 8th of each month in honor of Mary’s Immaculate Conception and in imitation of the foundress.

It is penance that creates in us readiness for and attraction to prayer.

“Jesus spent the nights in prayer.”

Mother Rosa too loved the silence of the night for prayer.

In her little room and before the Blessed Sacrament.

One evening she saw the sacristan leave after finishing her duties without spending a little time in adoration.

“Sister, at least say three Glory Be’s before you leave.”

After Communion she would remain in thanksgiving for about an hour, kneeling on the floor with one arm resting on a chair, motionless. No one was to disturb her, for any reason.

“What do you say to the Lord for so long?”

“Before Jesus time has no time.”

To a Sister who wrote to her about her difficulties she replied:

“Why don’t you run to the heart of Jesus? There you will find true comfort and draw grace to continue on the Lord’s way.”

A lighted candle cannot replace a backbone

“There are Catholics,” Arturo Paoli has written, “who could live their religion in 1200 or in 1800: time does not touch them at all. On the contrary, feeling spiritually fulfilled makes them safe and snatches them from the responsibility — an atrocious one, certainly — of their time.

“They feel the fixity of the commandments of Sinai, the implacable force of God’s command, but history does not touch them.

“They feel bound to practice justice, but any justice; to believe in freedom, but any freedom. ‘Prophecy’, on the other hand, means understanding history.

“The prophet is one who has grasped the deep meaning of God’s word in the historical situation in which God has called him as witness. He is sent by God to decipher events and discern God’s revelation in them.”

For Rosa Gattorno “understanding history” meant thinking of those who at that moment were most in need: the sick, the insane, prisoners.

Love of God flowers in love of neighbor.79

An underfed people produces neither philosophers nor saints.

“The spiritual always lies in the bed of the temporal” (Péguy).

On her journeys Rosa Gattorno never failed to visit the poor inmates entrusted to her Daughters and to commend them warmly to their zeal.

“Mother... unfortunately there’s little to be done with certain jailbirds...”

“No,” she replied. “If you manage to prevent sin for just one hour, that will be a great gain before God.”

Her favorite place was beside souls in danger of being lost. From the testimony of Canon Pietro Tosti of Foligno we know that in 1873, just after the house of the Daughters of Saint Anne opened in that town, the Servant of God was asked to nurse a young man who was seriously ill, a victim of his vices, and so hostile to religion that he had two friends guard him to keep the priest out.

For the first nights Rosa Gattorno confined herself to caring for his body, to win his heart.

But at the right moment she spoke to him so effectively of the spiritual remedy that he declared his intention to go to confession and prepared very well, often asking to kiss the crucifix.

But how could a priest get in? Mother Rosa asked him when his guards would leave him alone, even briefly; he replied not before one or two in the morning. So she made arrangements with the cathedral parish priest and brought him to the sick man in those free hours. The man confessed with such jubilation that he was beside himself with joy, and serenely exclaimed: “Now I am happy!”

The two men, seeing they had been outwitted, were furious and resolved to take revenge.

One morning they attacked Mother Rosa as she left the house to go to Mass. She screamed and managed to escape their dagger.

A few days later a magistrate of the town sent for her.

“Mother, given the way the wind is blowing, wouldn’t it be better for you to leave town?...”

“Me? Not on your life... If I had done something wrong... but since I’ve done nothing wrong, why should I leave?”

So much for a pious, simpering Rosa Gattorno.

She certainly had a backbone...

“A lighted candle cannot replace a backbone” (A. Paoli).

She told her Sisters: “When you find a patient who does not ask for the sacraments, don’t waste words, but do everything for him in such a way that he is filled with admiration. Go to him often, so as to anticipate his wishes, and you will see that he himself will ask for the sacraments.”

And things often turned out just like that.

“Where did you learn such charity? Who taught you? Not even my mother or sister would have done so much”: so the patients at the hospital of Borgo S. Donnino told Sr A. Camilla Valentini.

The Daughters of Saint Anne had understood well what the apostolate is.

The apostolate is not so much doing as being.

Today’s world is terribly suspicious of the spoken and written word. Words have been used too falsely. People today hear them and at once go on the alert, adopting a mentality of distrust.80

But before the word embodied in life — that is, witness — they surrender.

“Gospel teaching is so lofty that people need to see it embodied in someone to believe it can be lived in everyday life. That is the task, the commitment, of witnesses, who shout the Gospel with their lives.”

To shout the Gospel from the rooftops with one’s life: that was the motto adopted by Fr de Foucauld.

The whole problem lies here: it is precisely a matter of carrying the Gospel over, translating it into our lives. Let not a single page remain only on paper.

“One must not imagine that one can effectively be the priest of a religion of which one has not first been a faithful follower.”

“The true apostolate is not talking but being. Today the chattering apostolate is in fashion. Our apostolate is holiness. Every soul that rises raises the world” (Sister Geneviève Gallois).

This page of Mauriac is worth meditating on: “People have been deceived too often: it is not words that still have a grip on them today, it is example. Not the word of God commented on or updated to the taste of the day, but the Son of Man, the Word of life, seen and touched in the person of a poor creature living among the poor, like them, who makes shine in his person that Presence before which the man born blind falls on his knees: ‘Jesus, having found him, said: Do you believe in the Son of God? He answered: And who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him? Jesus said to him: You have seen him, and it is he who speaks to you. [I] believe, Lord, he said, and he fell at his feet and worshipped him’ (Jn 9:35-38).”

We do not know whether or when Mother Rosa will work miracles. It is for the Church to pronounce on that.

But one miracle she has already worked, in the etymological sense of the word: “miracle”, something that makes us marvel.

Her virtues, her sufferings and her works are Rosa Gattorno’s first miracle.

A workman once said of a priest: “When you met him you felt like kneeling down.”

That is the whole portrait of the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno.

“The renewal of religious life involves a constant return to the sources of all Christian life and to the original spirit of the institutes, and at the same time their adaptation to the changed conditions of the times...”

The Church of the Council said:

“... since the fundamental norm of religious life is the following of Christ as set forth in the Gospel...” (PC 2).

“The religious state more faithfully imitates and continually represents in the Church the form of life which the Son of God accepted in entering this world to do the will of the Father and which he proposed to the disciples who followed him...” (LG 44).

Mother Gattorno wrote:

“The Daughters of Saint Anne... will always mirror themselves in their Spouse Jesus, to see in him the model by which they must adorn themselves, the model to imitate in practicing that evangelical charity counselled and practiced by our Redeemer, and dear and holy humility.”

“All the Daughters must keep before them the divine Model, Jesus, to correct their way of thinking and acting, especially regarding that charity I so strongly recommend...”

“If we want to learn, we must always keep the figure of the Redeemer before our eyes and look at it constantly; then we shall do everything perfectly.”

“The Lord is our help and our Master and knows how to teach us well. Let us try to profit from his lessons and be diligent pupils, so as to please him and fulfill his will completely.”

The Church of the Council:

“Those who profess the evangelical counsels should seek and love above all else God who has first loved us, and in all circumstances they should strive to foster a life hidden with Christ in God, which is the source and stimulus of love of neighbor for the salvation of the world and the building up of the Church” (PC 6).

Mother Gattorno:

“If you knew, my daughter, how much Jesus loves you, you would surely be mad about him and do nothing but say to him: ‘My Love, speak to me, command me, for I want to do everything that pleases you.’”

“... my portion is charity.”

“‘Love, love, and then do what you will,’ says St Augustine. Yes, whoever loves cannot displease the Beloved, so in everything she does she has a sweet fear of erring and displeasing: holy fear, sweet and dear, you are nothing but a chain binding me to the Heart of Love.”

“I want one thing from you: that you strive to love God with a love that is wholly pure, ardent and on fire. If you reach that, I will tell you: do what you will, and you will do everything well. ‘Love and do what you will,’ said St Augustine. Yes, my daughter, love this God and Father and you will do everything gladly.”

“Let us see creatures in him and love them.”

“Take comfort, you who toil for your Jesus, because in touching the sick with charity, in touching those ailing creatures, you touch Jesus who is in them.”
