“Let us hope that good Jesus will deign to let himself be nursed by the poor Daughters of Saint Anne.”

“Dear Daughters of Saint Anne, love, love Jesus; make yourselves victims of charity. I envy you!”

“... There is a charity more sublime, more delicate, greater, and very dear to our crucified Lord. What is this charity? When a person strips herself of what she needs and gives it away... The Church of the Council:

“... apostolic and charitable activity belongs to the very nature of religious life, seeing that it is a holy service and a work of charity entrusted to them by the Church and to be carried out in her name... Mother Gattorno:

“You always have a way to meditate, seeing Jesus in the sick...”

“Peace, my daughters, peace, silence, calm: then you will hear God coming to speak to your hearts with loving, sweet words.”

“My Jesus, what should be closer to your heart than that your Father be glorified in this Work? “To carry out their chief task well — nursing the sick day and night — the Daughters of Saint Anne must exercise the spirit of faith that sees Jesus Christ in the person of the sick; the spirit of hope that seeks all reward in God, in the resurrection and the glory of Paradise; the spirit of love that leads them, while caring for the sick in body, to encourage them to use their illness as a means of penance for their sins, to receive the sacraments and to die the death of the elect.”

The Church of the Council:

“Chastity embraced for the sake of the kingdom of heaven... frees the heart of man so that he becomes more fervent in love for God and for all men... (it is) a most effective means given to religious to dedicate themselves generously to the divine service and the works of the apostolate” (PC 12).

Mother Gattorno:

“Try to detach yourself from all earthly affections and live for God alone. Then you will be a true Daughter of Saint Anne.”

“Once we have given ourselves to the Lord, he does not want us to have any more dealings with earthly things, but to raise our minds to him alone: he becomes jealous.”

The Church of the Council:

Mother Gattorno:

“My daughter, look at Jesus in the stable at Bethlehem: there was no bed, only straw! Yet the Son of God chose it as his first dwelling and willed to be born there! “My blessed daughters, stand firm and trust wholly in God; love your privations, the discomfort your human nature must bear: treasure these riches and joyfully offer them to your Eternal Father, that he may deign to bless and keep them...”

“‘Yes, we are poor and we rejoice in it!’ Oh, if I heard the Daughters of Saint Anne say that, how happy I would be!”

The Church of the Council:

“The institutes themselves... should strive to bear a quasi-collective witness to poverty and should willingly devote part of their goods to the other needs of the Church and to the support of the poor...” (PC 13).

Mother Gattorno:

(In the Institute) “nothing may be accumulated, since any surplus must be distributed to the poor and to needy churches...”

“Pray to obtain from God both providence and the gift of practicing and loving poverty and tasting this treasure; and meanwhile promise him that with his divine help you will practice it.”

The Church of the Council:

“... nor should they neglect the natural means which promote mental and bodily health” (PC 12).

Mother Gattorno:

“My daughter, try to look after yourself and get strong, or you won’t be fit to serve God.”

Mother Gattorno:

“What does obedience mean for us? I seem to hear a voice saying to me: In love you will find what this virtue demands of you.”

“What consolation I feel just saying the words: ‘to please God’! And even more, when the thought awakens in me that I am or could become his delight, I am beside myself, so that if I had to face the cruellest martyrdom I would feel nothing.”

Mother Gattorno:

“Prudence, gentleness, charity: with these three virtues, my daughter, you will lead the Daughters of Saint Anne along the way of perfection.”

“My daughters, try to be the servants of all!”

Courage: suffering is indispensable. Look at Peter: “Come,” the Master said to him. And without thinking whether he had a family or anything else, he ran at once. So did all who followed the Savior. This Master certainly had no other pastime than going in search of the lost sheep, heedless of food or clothing; and with him the Apostles went hungry and thirsty; to say it all in a word, suffering was their mission.

My daughter, today I received your anguished letter; what am I to reply? Only that for whoever wants to follow Jesus this is the way: to suffer and toil.

One may say that our Master began his sufferings, his terrible agony, on the first day of his life.

My system is not to rejoice too much in contentments but to find true joy in the adversities and crosses Jesus sends us and which, as Master, he teaches us to embrace.

Prayer is the key to graces; it opens the Lord’s treasures.

Sincerity, charity, the love of God are all we need; everything else is nothing at all.

Believe me, my daughters, I have no sins of idleness — perhaps the only ones I shall not find at God’s judgment seat.

In some cases, my daughter, you must decide for yourself: first commend yourself to God, then go forward with courage.

Let us bless the Lord for giving us the grace to rest our hopes in him alone.

How gladly one serves this dear Master, so gentle in his commands and content with everything, provided our actions are upright and done solely to please him and serve him as he deserves.

May God give you strength to do everything well, but for him alone; we want nothing else.

Let us place ourselves in God’s presence and receive everything from his hands. Let us hold to the conviction that in all we do in this Work we are directed by him; so if we find some good done, we know it comes from our Creator’s hands. But if we see ourselves at fault in anything, and what we have done has turned out badly, let us be sure it is our own work and that good Jesus allows it to make us feel that every time we turn away from him we are good for nothing.

Let us trust in God; since the Work is his, he will provide for everything.

Courage and patience! The Lord will soon come with special providence. I do not lack the least trust in God the Father. When we least expect it, he will provide. Meanwhile let us pray fervently, so that our prayers may reach the loving heart of Jesus; there lies the source of all spiritual and temporal riches.

“Providence” will come; don’t worry, my daughter; God will think of us if we think only of him. Repeat the prayer for “providence” to St Joseph, and ask him to give you humility, and through that virtue to give you providence.

Stay humble, for this is the only way not to fall and to become holy.

Humility, you are the queen of all virtues!

Dear Eternal Father, will you grant this wretched creature, before she dies, the consolation of seeing this beautiful jewel shine in all your daughters and mine in the house of glorious Saint Anne? Then indeed my head will rest happily on the pillow of death!

Let truth always be on your lips and simplicity in your hearts.

Let truth be your treasure, always.

My daughter, whenever you have to speak, don’t think too anxiously about what to answer, trying to use your own wits. No, no — present yourself to anyone without study, except the study of charity and gentleness, but without affectation, simply, united with God. Then speak without fear, and you will say everything well.

O sweet Jesus, whoever loves you knows how to speak well! So, my daughter, love and do what you will, and you will do everything well.

Pray and have others pray that I may keep peace and joy alive even under the weight of so heavy a cross.

To carry the cross well one needs strength, courage and generosity.

Love Jesus and be content; Jesus wants to be served with joy.

For Jesus we must bear everything cheerfully.

Sorrows turn to joy when one suffers for Our Lord.

My daughter, be at peace, for peace of soul, together with bodily calm and perfect resignation to God’s will, does our poor human nature much good.

And what happens to angry people? They ruin their livers and soon become unfit for any service. Courage and peace: let them be your faithful guardians.

Jesus loves the courageous. He is pleased to lay part of his cross on their shoulders. But let us trust in him, for this is the only way to run safely along the road to heaven.

My daughter, do not fail to act with strength and courage, without human respect.

Speak little and pray much; you will be glad of it not only on the day of judgment but now too, for in silence the soul can converse with Jesus, always finds her Spouse and enjoys union with him.

My daughter, if I were to consider the risk to myself, it would certainly be rash to undertake so long a journey, for humanly speaking I have no hope of health left; but if God so commands, I go, relying on his providence.

Among the founders who marked nineteenth-century Italy, Mother Rosa Gattorno holds a place of special prominence. A most tender wife and mother, immersed in her time and its problems, she accomplished in a few short years an apostolic work of vast dimensions. Her secret is simple: to be conformed to Christ in suffering, in humility, in a loving embrace of every creature.

A woman in the fullest sense of the word, driven by a devouring charity, severe with herself and full of understanding for others, Rosa Gattorno left a deep mark on the fabric of Italian Catholicism through an example and witness of rare power. That is why it is fitting today to look closely at the experience of this extraordinary woman. Our historical moment suffers a crisis of witness: words, debates or, worse, apathy and indifference seem to have dulled the will to love and the boldness of deeds, the willingness to take on responsibility even when it hurts, the capacity to suffer and, if need be, to die for love. We play with “crises”, listen to our own anxieties, lament a world without God. But “if God exists,” a workman told a French priest, “he is what you do.” God’s face shows through our witness. But witness does not mean shouting “Fire!” in one’s slippers; it means throwing oneself into the blaze, ready to lose everything, becoming “servant of the servants”, making oneself “all things to all”. Seen in this light, the figure of Mother Rosa Gattorno towers above us and shows our timid consciences the road to follow to be Christians to the very end.

Prostrate at the feet of this Sovereign and Queen of sorrows, weeping bitterly, I said to her: ‘Must I abandon my children? Your Son, through his Vicar, commands it of me. I feel torn apart with grief; I love them so much! You, my Mother, knew what it was to lose Jesus: just losing him for three days, what it cost you!
